Title: Governor's speech at the Finance Summit on 19 April 2016
text: Governor's speech at the Finance Summit on April 19, 2016 Governor's speech at the Finance Summit on 19 April 2016 Ladies / Gentlemen I am delighted that I have the opportunity I have today at this forum, which is distinguished by its rich reflections on the major issues affecting our economic and financial realities, to associate myself with this very commendable and useful initiative. I feel all the more honored because I have the mission to deliver the inaugural address in one of the most popular sessions of these meetings. 2011-2016, here we are at the sixth edition of the Finance Summit. This event is therefore resolutely confirmed as the forum where practitioners and academics from various backgrounds meet to take stock and identify perspectives in the fields of economics, finance and public policies in general. First of all, I would like to salute the steadfastness of the Growth Group and the determination of its CEO, Mr. Kesner Pharel who was able to maintain regularity in the organization of this event, despite the adversities of a difficult and uncertain environment. It is important to remember that the first edition took place only one year after the shock of 2010, in a particular context marked by the enormous human, economic and infrastructure costs incurred by our society as well as the effects, at the time, of a collapsed economy that had just lost 120% of its GDP. Even today, the sixth edition is taking place in a context of political transition that hinders the normal functioning of companies and institutions. These are enormous constraints where the authorities must, on the one hand, make a tight trade-off between the many priority needs in relation to increasingly limited resources, and on the other hand, manage the pessimistic expectations that find expression in the rapid increase in the exchange rate and the rise in inflationary pressures. These pessimistic expectations, it should be remembered, are regularly fuelled by uncertainties that increase risk premia in a context of endogenous shocks and multiple exogenous shocks. Whether they are linked, for example, to the fall in the world price of oil and its impact on the resources available for financing public investments or to climate disasters that severely affect agricultural production, thus increasing the volatility of relative prices. Dear friends, The theme under which the event takes place this year refers to two issues, two deficits that concern two key variables and often joined by interaction in the process of development of our economy: the financing deficit and the infrastructure deficit. Indeed, the needs for road, energy, agricultural and production infrastructure in general are immense and their implementation is constrained by the lack of funds available at the Government level and the insufficiency of those devoted by the banking and financial industry to their development. The primary role of infrastructure in creating the conditions for a path of sustainable and inclusive growth cannot be overemphasized. For this, reforms are needed at several levels to adapt banking resources, usually short-term, to the financing of these large-scale projects; diversifying sources of financing by deepening the money market; promote the creation of a viable financial market and a capital market with risk-sharing institutions in long-term investments. The banking law of 2012 already provides the legal framework for the operation of finance companies under the supervision of the Central Bank and we are currently working on the establishment of a structure within the BRH to deal with the creation and supervision of a capital market. We are delighted that the meetings of this sixth edition of the Finance Summit will be the ideal place to feed the reflections that must support actions to advance this agenda. Ladies and Gentlemen, The BRH is pleased with the faithful support it has provided, since the beginning, to the organization of the various editions of the Finance Summit. It also welcomes its active participation in the sustained and interesting discussions that animate the sessions because it is aware that the information, added value and insights provided by reflections on economic choices and the orientation of public policies are useful for policymakers, investors and economic agents in general. We are convinced that to form coherent and rational expectations, an economic agent needs to be informed and trained. All the information at its disposal must be enriched both by the data conveyed by the markets and any reflections on public policy and monetary policy issues in particular that affect its way of allocating resources. As such, the BRH's interest in the Finance Summit is part of the institution's desire to reduce information asymmetry through more intense communication, necessary for a better transmission mechanism and better effectiveness of monetary policy. The fact that different public and private entities engage in this exercise, which consists of discussing economic and financial issues and identifying perspectives, could not be more useful in laying the basis for the information efficiency of markets to progress on an upward curve. The Finance Summit thus creates a space for inter-institutional dialogue and reflects what should be an obligation of transparency of public policy agendas to the agents and institutions concerned by their implementation. In this sense, the BRH will continue to support all initiatives contributing to a greater dissemination of information in order to reduce the information divide that prevents markets to express the truth of prices. This is the wish of the Board of Directors of the BRH, which I have the honour to chair, and which is also working on a set of projects, some of which sometimes conflict with the traditional orthodoxy of central banks. These projects are justified in the context of a small, low-income economy in which we are committed to providing institutional support to actors and productive sectors, which is essential for increasing overall added value. Indeed, contemplating the need to boost local production, including agricultural production, our approach, while imposing no constraint on the current sectoral distribution of credit, aims to put in place incentives for credit to strategic sectors and high added value. In addition, we emphasize ways to gradually reduce the balance of payments current account deficit by creating favourable conditions for export enterprises. We believe that it is also appropriate to support the private production sector by strengthening technical support, particularly with regard to vocational formation. This is a solid foundation for job creation and economic growth, bearing in mind the role of human capital in endogenous growth models and then the obligations linked to our legislated mission to take all initiatives to promote economic growth. In general, a stable socio-political environment and the resolution of economic imbalances are necessary for macroeconomic stability and sustainable exchange rate stability. In the current context where these two conditions present themselves as challenges, the BRH, while continuing to maintain the use of its traditional monetary policy instruments, is working on ways to add to its posture measures in the direction of the attractiveness of the gourde in order to encourage savings in local currency and reduce the rate of impatience of agents in their supply of dollars. We are also working on the establishment of permanent mechanisms for the popularization of economic and financial information as a central element of our desire to contribute to the effectiveness and implementation of the national financial inclusion strategy. Ladies and gentlemen, this is a set of non-exhaustive projects, either under implementation or under study, on which I am working with my colleagues on the Board of Directors and my team at the BRH, and of which we can, at the appropriate time, make an assessment of progress and achievement. Finally, I congratulate Mr Pharel once again for having created this necessary space for dialogue between economic actors. I also congratulate the winners of the various editions of the Summit who have marked the world of finance in Haiti by paying tribute to the memory of Guito Toussaint, Henri Bazin and Lhermite Francois who left too soon. Thank you for your attention Thank you

Title: Installation speech by the Governor of the BRH
text: Installation speech by the Governor of the BRH Installation speech by the Governor of the BRH Mr. President of the Senate Mr. Prime Minister Minister of Economy and Finance Outgoing Governor and Member Ladies / Gentlemen of the Board of Directors Representatives of the banking system BRH executives Dear Guest-Associates First of all, I would like to express my thanks to the President of the Republic, His Excellency Joseph Michel Martelly, for having chosen me to take the reins of the Bank of the Republic of Haiti in a context marked by many socio-economic, monetary and financial challenges. This is proof of a great confidence that I appreciate very much and that I will strive to honour. My thanks also go to Prime Minister Evans Paul, who has always supported the efforts of the institution and who accompanies the monetary and financial authorities in the quest for macroeconomic stability. Ladies and Gentlemen, In accordance with the missions entrusted to it by the law of August 17, 1979, the Bank of the Republic of Haiti has always oriented its policy towards the protection of the internal and external value of the national currency, has been able to maintain the stable and profitable financial system, has undertaken a set of initiatives to promote credit essential to growth and economic development. However, the current economic environment is characterized by a sharp acceleration of the exchange rate, a slowdown in economic activities and a trend towards renewed inflationary pressures. This is, in addition to the significant influence of cyclical factors, the result of a set of persistent constraints and several decades of macroeconomic imbalances: from trade balance deficits to pressures of the immensity of social needs on public finances, low national savings and the lack of resources for financing investment projects, an inadequate pace of national income in relation to population growth. These structural imbalances have fuelled the dollarization and depreciation of the gourde since the abandonment of the fixed parity regime. Over the past 30 years, public policies have focused mainly on macroeconomic consolidation and stabilization efforts. Historically, monetary policy has been able to cautiously accommodate the various constraints of the macroeconomic environment. In terms of results, inflation has been brought under control and brought down for a long time in the single digit range. After January 2010, the rate of depreciation of the gourde had slowed substantially and the exchange rate had even fallen significantly (42 gourdes in September 2009 to about 39 gourdes to the dollar in December 2010) thanks to incoming foreign exchange flows including humanitarian aid and public transfers, which have also declined significantly over the past two years. However, these policies have not solved the problems of growth and competitiveness and have not brought GDP closer to its potential level. Thus, monetary and other public policies must now focus on pro-growth, inclusive, capital accumulation measures at the national level but especially at the regional and local levels. They must result in redistributive effects that are likely to create opportunities, jobs and subsequently broaden the tax base fueling a virtuous circle of wealth creation, better public finances, breaking with the cycle of poverty. Dear friends, Having been at the Central Bank for twenty years and on the Board of Directors for about 4 years, I am aware of the immensity of the task at hand, the importance of the challenges to be met, the tight constraints under which it will be necessary to maximize the utility that economic agents, investors and households must derive from a stable exchange rate and inflation rate that are in fact only public goods. On the monetary and financial front, the BRH has achieved significant results in terms of financial stability, availability of means of payment, control of inflation as mentioned above, credit growth and is promoting, with the cooperation of the financial system, initiatives aimed at financial inclusion, the development of favorable conditions for the real estate sector and the productive sectors. In this regard, I must commend the work done by the outgoing Governor, Mr. Charles Castel during his term as Director General between 2004 and 2006 and as Governor from 2006 to 2015. Under his leadership, the BRH has, among other things, strengthened its modernization and decision-making process in monetary policy, contributed to efforts to safeguard the national cultural heritage, contributed with the Ministry of Economy and Finance to macroeconomic stabilization, maintained the stable financial system, held multiple national and international conferences. I also salute the enriching contributions of the outgoing Member, Mr. Fritz Duroseau, who is a sure value for the country, a reservoir of ideas, a model of rigour, of work. Well done, which the next generation will have to be inspired but also a model of humor that helps manage ambient stress. Nevertheless, despite the many achievements of the BRH at the monetary policy and institutional levels, it is imperative today to focus in particular on: Financial deepening through the creation of a financial market in Haiti because, on the one hand, the 2 billion dollar deposits and the 75 billion gourde deposits in the banking system will not be enough to finance the development of the country, and on the other hand, companies must also be able to finance themselves outside the money market, Economic agents must be able to find other alternatives for investing their monetary assets, apart from term deposits or savings deposits, which are also subject to the asymmetric effects of money transmission channels, companies must be able to finance themselves outside the money market. Some innovations in monetary policy and the application of prudential standards, such as regional differentiation of reserve requirements, which are already increasingly incorporating sectoral incentives. One systematization of the Guarantee Fund approach, which will be considered on a broader scale in terms of productive sectors to be integrated and encouraged; we will seek a more substantial commitment from the Haitian State and donors in terms of financial support. The establishment of a deposit insurance system to secure savers' assets in the event of the failure of a financial institution. The experiences of cooperatives in the early 2000s were quite trying. Financial services consumer protection. At the institutional level, consumer protection has not been explicitly integrated into all the missions assigned to the Central Bank in the law of 17 August 1979. In fact, there is a Office for the Protection of the Citizen which does not seem to have a specific vocation of consumer protection. However, in economic and financial terms, markets and the system of free competition contain many distortions that often harm the interests of individual economic agents. For example, the pricing of financial services, the transfer market, among others, should be given special attention to make them more transparent for users. The BRH must therefore extend the scope of surveillance to address these concerns. Consumer protection is also one of the pillars of financial inclusion currently being promoted by the institution. The establishment of a regular communication policy intended to inform economic agents and stake holders, to inform them about the actions of the Central Bank in order to help them better train and discipline their expectations. This is a fundamental element in the behaviour of markets and in the effectiveness of monetary policy; to name but a few. Ladies and Gentlemen, I accept to take charge of the management of the Central Bank in a context of great complexity of the monetary policy environment where socio-political tensions weigh on the formation of expectations and keep the economy in good condition. In particular, the recent evolution of the exchange rate manifested by the sharp depreciation of the gourde challenges the policy maker, not only the central banker. My institutional position is that the Central Bank cannot allow the exchange rate to go in search of competitiveness whose foundations have not yet been established. It will therefore continue to contain movements in the discount of the national currency by means of measures to create an attractiveness of the gourde to complement the current instruments of monetary policy. I will work closely with the Minister of Economy and Finance to strengthen the coordination of monetary and fiscal policies, which is necessary for more effective results. The institutional dialogue with the Professional Association of Banks will be strengthened and the members of the Board of Directors will remain attentive to the banking system for everything that can contribute to the efficiency of intermediation activities. Finally, I invite staff members to play their part in the mission entrusted to the institution and to respect the rules of ethics and integrity that have always characterized the Bank of the Republic of Haiti. Competence and performance are the compass that will guide the action of the Board of Directors. Thank you

Title: Speech on the occasion of the launch of the PRONAP (National Payment Processor) project
text: Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois on the occasion of the launch of the PRONAP project (National Payment Processor) Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois on the occasion of the launch of the PRONAP (National Payment Processor) project Distinguished representatives of the various financial institutions, Dear colleagues of the BRH Board of Directors, Mr. David Jacobs, consultant from Nexus Firm, here today, Members of the Steering Committee and the Technical Committee of the PRONAP project, Dear Central Bank Executives, We are very pleased to welcome you to the BRH Convention and Documentation Center for this meeting to launch the implementation phase of the PRONAP project (the National Payment Processor). It is also an opportunity to express the importance that the Board of Directors of the Bank of the Republic of Haiti attaches to this project, whose two main objectives are: On the one hand, to provide the country with modern payment and settlement infrastructures. In addition, this PRONAP project will ensure interoperability between the different means of payment and the different financial actors. On the other hand, to promote financial inclusion through retail payments. We want to see in the not too distant future, the small fruit merchant of Petion Ville, the shop on the corner of rue St Honore, the artist or craftsman of Boutilliers, the seller of Douce Macosse in Petit Goave, the farmer of Value receive payment for their goods through a debit card issued by the bank or the credit union of his customer in complete security and with the same level service of a luxury boutique in Petion Ville or a large supermarket. Let me remind you that since 2007, the BRH has been engaged in reforms aimed at modernizing the Haitian payment system: First, by the establishment of the RTGS, known by the financial community as SPIH, which represents the cornerstone of the Haitian payment system, then the clearing system based on the image of cheques, operational since 2013, then the circular on remote banking regulating mobile payment, finally the implementation for the local settlement of domestic transactions initiated by credit card, which will become a reality in two days, on July 29, 2016, for MasterCard cards and in about two months for VISA cards. Today, with the PRONAP Project, BRH wants to create the conditions for the development of an innovative retail payment system. It offers a platform for electronic payment services, which will broaden the choice of efficient and reliable payment instruments. This is an ambitious goal to facilitate access to quality payment services for all Haitians across the country. Nevertheless, this objective cannot be achieved without the support of the intermediaries of the payment system: banks and credit unions, which are the entities of the payment value chain in contact with the population. Despite the difficulties, the efforts of financial institutions to invest in retail payment methods such as bank cards, the deployment of ATM and POS networks are remarkable and date back more than fifteen years. We are pleased today to congratulate these financial institutions for their innovation efforts through adapted and innovative instruments, such as: Lajan CASH, Unibank Tout Kote, Soge IZI... To name but a few. The BRH has always welcomed the investments made by these institutions in order to offer the population electronic payment services. Nevertheless, in this movement, the lack of interoperability remains a problem that BRH wishes to address and solve jointly with the stakeholders of the payment system. PRONAP being a platform of electronic payment services will be able to allow this interoperability, by facilitating: the integration of the various private electronic payment networks already operating on the market; the issuance of payment cards by all financial institutions authorized and willing to do so; the arrival of new "players" in the card payment landscape. We are able to confirm today that all the technical arrangements (software systems and expertise) have been brought together on our side, here at BRH, to launch this implementation phase. It is clear that your respective technology and operations teams, based on the projects you have already completed, have relevant knowledge and experience in the field of electronic payment. We are therefore convinced that good collaboration and the involvement of the men and women involved in the project will lead to success. I conclude this brief introduction with my hope that all financial institutions that will participate in PRONAP will actively engage alongside the BRH in order to make the implementation phase a success. Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for your attention and wish you a very good working session.

Title: Speech on the Economic and Financial Issues Related to the Fight against Money Laundering and the Financing of Terrorism
text: Speech by the Governor of the BRH Mr. Jean Baden Dubois on the Economic and Financial Issues Related to the Fight against Money Laundering and the Financing of Terrorism Speech by the Governor of the BRH Mr. Jean Baden Dubois on the Economic and Financial Issues Related to the Fight against Money Laundering and the Financing of Terrorism Honourable President of the Senate and the National Assembly, Mr. Minister of Justice and Public Security, Mr. Minister of Economy and Finance, Mr. Chief of Staff of the Prime Minister, Mrs. and Mr. Members of the Cabinet of the President of the Republic, Dear Presidents of the Senate and Chamber of Deputies Committees, Honourable Senators and Deputies, Honourable Magistrates of the Superior Council of the Judiciary, Mr. Director General of the Central Financial Intelligence Unit (UCREF), Mr. Director General of the Anti-Corruption Unit (ULCC), Mr. Coordinator of the National Commission for the Fight against Drugs (CONALD), Mr. Director General of the National Police of Haiti, Members of the National Commission for the Fight against Asset Laundering (CNLBA), Dear colleagues of the Board of Directors of the Bank of the Republic of Haiti, Ladies and gentlemen of the banking sector and financial institutions, Ladies and gentlemen of the private business sector, Ladies and gentlemen, I would first like to express my warmest thanks to all the personalities who kindly responded to the joint invitation of the Ministry of Justice and the BRH and to honor us with their presence at this meeting-debate on the theme of money laundering. This reflects not only their interest in this subject but also, and above all, the willingness of national authorities to understand the fight against money laundering and the financing of terrorism in its financial and criminal aspects. This activity is part of the strengthening of the Haitian anti-money laundering system with the objective of following up on the commitments made by the State to make the necessary corrections before the next plenary meeting of the Caribbean Financial Action Task Force (CFATF) to be held next November. This morning's meeting responds, to a large extent, to the concerns expressed and demands made by the private business sector, the banking sector and the powers of the State. This initiative is particularly aimed at raising awareness among the various actors concerned of the importance of putting in place an adequate system, in accordance with the international standards of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the international conventions ratified by Haiti and the imperative need to adapt the legal mechanisms for the prevention, detection and suppression of money laundering and terrorist financing. Today's debate is also part of a sensitive context in which the CFATF issued a public statement last June highlighting the existing deficiencies of the Haitian system and inviting the country to take measures to remedy them. In this perspective, apart from structural and regulatory measures, it is fundamental that the legislature once again follows suit and joins the ranks of actors involved in the fight. Indeed, the undeniable partition of our parliamentarians has more than once been played out previously in the context of the adoption of the law of 21 February 2001 on the laundering of assets derived from illicit drug trafficking and serious crimes, the law of 14 May 2012 on banks and other financial institutions and recently that of 11 November 2013 sanctioning money laundering and the financing of terrorism. These legislative advances have been important in the fight against money laundering, but insufficient in view of this evolving phenomenon, new and increasingly sophisticated manifestations of which still need to be stemmed. Indeed, financial crime and its perverse effects on the economy of a nation challenge all States and require the establishment and strengthening of prevention, detection and repression bodies. In this respect, consultation at the level of national actors is intended to be a sine qua non element of an effective approach to combating these scourges. At the level of the banking and financial system, the weakness of the anti-money laundering system may lead to its weakening by isolation at the international level in the event that the CFATF relayed by the FATF asks all countries to take vigilance measures against Haiti. The negative impact of any new public statement next November on Haiti will be characterized by a sharp slowdown in international financial transactions (transfer, letter of credit, etc.) due to the risks of termination of banking correspondence relations, also called the phenomenon of "de-risking" and may eventually lead to the financial isolation of the country. The BRH is therefore at the crossroads of prevention, in its mission of regulating and stabilizing the financial system. Financial institutions are the first line of defence in terms of prevention, which requires the BRH to regularly monitor the adequacy of its financial regulations and the effectiveness of supervisory instruments with regard to money laundering. The BRH has already endeavoured to update the entire regulatory corpus in order to ensure that financial institutions scrupulously discharge their duty of care towards customers as well as their reporting obligation vis-a-vis the Central Financial Intelligence Unit (UCREF). In conducting this long-term exercise, the BRH advocates in all respects the proper implementation of the FATF and Basel Committee recommendations, as well as the relevant provisions of the United Nations Security Council resolutions on the duty of vigilance. BRH also ensures the strengthening of its human resources capacity by ensuring the continuous training of its managers and by adopting the supervisory approach recommended by both the FATF and the Basel Committee with regard to money laundering. Ladies and Gentlemen, However, the contribution of the various actors involved in the fight against money laundering and terrorist financing must be collaborative and harmonious. Each actor is called upon to fulfil its role in strengthening the chain of prevention, detection and repression. The strategic action plan drawn up with CFATF technical assistance aims, inter alia, to strengthen the legislative framework through:  The amendment of the 2013 anti-money laundering law,  The adoption of an organic law for UCREF;  The adoption of the new penal code. The adoption of these laws will ensure compliance with certain international standards and conventions ratified by Haiti in this area, and strengthen the legislative framework. Ladies and Gentlemen, If the above-mentioned measures have not materialized before the November plenary, the country risks being put on the list of non-cooperative countries. This will result in the intensification of the phenomenon of de-risking within our financial system. The economic stakes are high in view of the current economic situation given Haiti's dependence on major US banks. If, for lack of action on our part, these banks decide to cease their relations with Haitian financial institutions, 93% of our exports, 75% of transfers received, 72% of transfers abroad would be significantly affected. In particular, we must think about the socio-economic impacts that this could have if the 2 billion US dollars in transfers, or 21% of our GDP, can no longer feed the income of the most vulnerable layers. In addition, nearly 40% of our imports come from the United States. Imagine a situation where these banks withdraw and our importers can no longer source from the international market. In addition, the increase in country risk will have a strong impact on the costs of foreign transactions and will have an impact on local prices, with adverse consequences for political and economic stability. Faced with these challenges, we must prioritize the actions to be taken within a reasonable time and take the necessary measures to prevent our beloved Haiti from being categorized among the nations putting the global financial system at risk and being quarantined by international financial institutions. Good participation to all. Thank you!

Title: Speech on the occasion of the installation of the new Board of Directors of the BRH
text: Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois on the occasion of the installation of the new Board of Directors of the BRH Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois on the occasion of the installation of the new Board of Directors of the BRH Your Excellency the Prime Minister Honourable President of the National Assembly Honourable Presidents of the Finance Committee of the Senate of the Republic and the Chamber of Deputies Honourable Members Minister of Economy and Finance Minister of Justice Madam President of the Court of Auditors and Administrative Litigation Ladies, Members of the Ministerial Cabinet Dear colleagues of the Board of Directors of the BRH Ladies / Gentlemen representatives of the financial system BRH executives Distinguished guests, Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a great honor for me to assume the presidency of the new Board of Directors of the Bank of the Republic of Haiti, after ratification by the Senate of the Republic. On behalf of my colleagues, I thank the President of the Republic, His Excellency Mr. Jocelerme Privert, the Prime Minister, His Excellency Mr. Enex Jean Charles, the Minister of Economy and Finance, Yves Bastien, and the honourable senators for their confidence in our integrity, our abilities and our determination to carry out the task entrusted to us for the next three years. This honour invites us to humility, in the face of this formidable mission, in the face of this delicate task of managing the country's money supply with maximum growth and minimum inflation, and we want to count on the full collaboration of the staff of the central bank, our partners in the BRH-APB Joint Committee, other financial institutions such as credit unions, our traditional public sector clients and our partners in the international community. Allow me to warmly salute the contributions of Ms. Yamilee Champagne to the implementation of what we have started to date. I wish her as much if not more success in future ventures to which she will bring her knowledge and know-how. I would also like to take this opportunity to welcome the return to the Board of Fritz Duroseau who is a former member of the Central Bank. Fritz, welcome to the team. Ladies and Gentlemen, The challenges ahead are enormous. Putting our economy on a sufficiently robust, sustained and inclusive growth path will not be an easy undertaking. Recent data show us that inflation can be contained, but at the cost of economic stagnation as unbearable as price volatility. In other words, the sacrifice ratio, the cost (in terms of unemployment and misery) of a fall in the inflation rate seems too high for society. Moreover, singularly complicating the dilemma, shocks and other recent events, such as droughts, erosion, emigration of skilled labor from Haiti to Brazil, Chile, Canada, the Dominican Republic, etc., have reduced the productive capacity of the economy to the point where total spending tends to affect prices more than output. Ladies and Gentlemen, Beyond the theoretical controversies and the sadness of reality, the Bank of the Republic of Haiti must remain faithful to its mandate to execute a monetary policy that maintains the level of production at the level of productive capacity, that is, to minimize unemployment and inflation. This is the course that the new Board of Directors intends to maintain for the well-being of the national community, in collaboration with the Ministry of Economy and Finance, within the framework of a constant and active coordination of monetary and fiscal policies. This is the time for us to welcome the extraordinary efforts of the executive branch to limit state spending within the limits of its revenues in order to prevent any fiscal slippage and detrimental to the stability and healthy growth of the economy. As I mentioned not long ago, this cash management program is proof of financial restraint on the part of the State and reflects a deep sense of fiscal responsibility that will serve as a model for future administrations. It is hoped that the private business sector will receive the signal appropriately; On the other hand, it is regrettable that the international community has chosen not to financially support such an economic effort. Ladies and Gentlemen, This fiscal posture  which is the opposite of fiscal dominance  allows the central bank to better control its monetary balance sheet and to manage liquidity, including credit, according to the legitimate needs of agents. On this point, we must be clear: the monetary discipline that this Council intends to follow has nothing to do with a monetarist orthodoxy blind to market imperfections and indifferent to unexpected exogenous shocks. Nevertheless, we remain confident in the ability of our institutions and parliamentarians to remedy this situation as soon as possible. The country deserves no less...... Thank you.

Title: Speech on the occasion of the opening of the Digital Economy Fair organized by CONATEL
text: Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois on the occasion of the opening of the Digital Economy Fair organized by CONATEL Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois on the occasion of the opening of the Digital Economy Fair organized by CONATEL Mr. Secretary of State for Public Works Honourable Chairman of the Public Works Committee of the Chamber of Deputies Mr. Director General of CONATEL Directors-General Mr. Representative of ITU, International Telecommunication Union Representative Representative of ICANN (Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers) Madam Representative of the World Bank in Haiti Senior Officials of the Public Administration Ladies and Gentlemen Representatives of Telecommunications Operators Representatives of Civil Society Ladies and Gentlemen I am really pleased to participate and exchange with you on an innovative theme: the digital economy and financial inclusion at the Salon de l'economie Numerique, a space that combines information and communication technologies, finance and the digital economy. According to the OECD and the Digital Observatory, the digital economy is an expression that covers very different realities according to the authors, especially since this name has evolved over the years: new technologies, NICTs, new economy, information and communication technologies, electronic economy. In the scheme of the digital economy, it is necessary to distinguish four categories of actors: 1. Companies in the sectors producing information and communication technology services (ICTS) within the meaning of the OECD, whose activities are carried out in the fields of computers, telecommunications and electronics. 2. Companies whose existence is linked to the emergence of ICT (online services, video games, e-commerce, online media and content, etc.). 3. Companies that use ICT in their activity and gain in productivity thanks to it (banks, insurance, automotive, aeronautics, distribution, administration and tourism...). 4. Individuals and households who use ICTs in their daily activities, for leisure, culture, health, education, banking, social networks. In the latest study published in May 2014, the Inter- American Development Bank (IDB) on broadband internet development in the 26 countries of Latin America and the Caribbean, Haiti is ranked last. Antonio Garcia Zaballos, head of telecommunications and broadband initiative at the IDB, said: "In a modern society, broadband is the key ingredient of public policy to accelerate economic growth and reduce inequality." The study estimates that a 10% penetration of broadband services in the region would translate into an average increase in gross domestic product (GDP) growth of 3.2% and 2.6% in productivity. He goes on to say: "The lack of coordination between the public and private sectors is increasing, particularly in Haiti, the digital divide between urban and rural areas. For Haiti to benefit from this technology, it is necessary for all stakeholders, including businesses, legislators and regulators to work together towards a common goal of bridging the digital divide." The Central Bank is today at the crossroads of technology and finance and is called by its role as financial regulator to accompany, to put in place the safeguards and sometimes to take the initiative for the expansion of any strategic sector of the economy. The digital economy is today a vector of growth, productivity and competitiveness of companies and countries. It is the transformation of information used or provided into digital information. The total contribution of the digital economy to the growth of countries is composed of a direct effect via the accumulation of digital capital and the indirect effect measured by the diffusion of digital capital in the productive system. The impact of digital on financial inclusion is the rapid evolution of digital financial services for the poor. Indeed, through financial inclusion, we aim to ensure the widest possible access to savings, credit and other financial products and services with the aim of reducing poverty and income inequality to foster a more financially and economically inclusive society. According to Mark Warshauer in his book: Technology and Social Inclusion: Rethinking the Digital Divide, "There are many similarities between literacy and access to ICTs. First, both literacy and access to ICTs are closely linked to advances in human communication and the means of knowledge production. Second, just as access to ICTs is a prerequisite for full participation in the information phase of capitalism, literacy was (and remains) a prerequisite for full participation in the industrial stages of capitalism. Third, literacy and access to ICTs require a connection to a physical element (a book or a computer or laptop), to sources of information that are expressed as content within or through that physical artifact, and to a level sufficient to process and make use of the skills of that information. Fourth, both involve not only receiving information, but also producing. Finally, they are both linked to somewhat controversial notions of social cleavages: the large literacy gap can accentuate the digital divide and vice versa. To enable the poorest segments of the population to have access to basic financial products, we need to think outside the box and adopt innovative solutions. It is necessary for the State to take into account structural shortcomings so that through digital technology our 80% of adults over the age of 15 have access to financial services. The low level of financial inclusion is a barrier to socio-economic development in developing countries. How can we talk about financial inclusion, if the economic agent cannot be identified, has no known address and is unable to access financial institutions? However, there are opportunities, 62% of the population over 15 years old in Haiti has a mobile phone. Thus, through this instrument, banking and non-bank financial institutions can more easily reach the unbanked, making digital a fast and effective way to boost financial inclusion. For Jeffrey Sachs, the eminent economist the mobile phone is "the most transformative technology for development". The World Bank's flagship publication on Information and Communication Technologies for Development (ICT4D) makes a similar remark: "Mobile communication has arguably had a greater impact on humanity in a shorter period of time than any other invention in human history." The advent of the mobile phone has therefore greatly contributed to reducing the digital divide and offers an unprecedented opportunity to developing countries like Haiti, a gateway to social inclusion. The costs of accessing large global networks are thus reduced through the use of mobile technology versus fixed technology or desktop or laptop computers for several reasons. I can name at least 5 reasons: a) It is an inexpensive device: mobile Internet experiences are possible on devices that are often cheaper than "fixed" devices  specifically workstations (PCs). The cost of the workstation plays a huge role in determining the form and extent of access. In the majority of cases, people want mobile handsets  to make phone calls, send text, save photos and the like  so the additional cost for the user to acquire a device with a data connection is often zero. b) Usage-based pricing: A customer no longer needs to have a bank account or credit card, address or credit profile to access the network. A prepaid card is enough, "pap padap" or "la pou la". Instead, they pay by adding credits, small packets of airtime, in the telecommunications services that are within their reach. c) Wireless connections: Thus, mobile communication reduces the cost of initial phone service connectivity in most cases, for most users and has helped make the initial costs of voice connectivity affordable for billions of people. The same thing is happening now with Internet access, for people like the student, the farmer who could not afford a fixed broadband connection. d) It's personal: Unlike a fixed connection, the mobile often allows you to create a personal and intimate relationship. Users create strong connections with their small devices, screens, and interfaces designed for one user at a time and often for a single owner. Mobile phones have been designed, sold and bought from the beginning to be transported from one place to another, from home to work, and vice versa, living in our pockets and purses. e) It's universal: The mobile phone has sold billions of units, because, it seems, almost everyone wants to connect, to be in touch with colleagues, friends and loved ones and to feel safe in case of emergency. Mobile telephony has therefore paved the way for social inclusion and certainly for financial inclusion. Ladies and gentlemen, the digital economy combined with financial inclusion or digital financial inclusion is "the result of digital access to and use of formal financial services by previously excluded or underserved populations". Based on the above, BRH together with the World Bank has developed its national financial inclusion strategy around five pillars: These five pillars aim to improve the availability, accessibility and quality of financial services provided to the above-mentioned target groups. Specifically: Pillar 1  Financial Services for Inclusion and Poverty Reduction  supporting the delivery of financial services to low-income individuals and households income, including savings and credit products, government payments to individuals, transfers, micro-insurance and micro-pensions. Pillar 2  Credit for Economic Growth  We will encourage the development of MSME (Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises) finance, agricultural finance, and housing finance, including insurance instruments to help manage risks. Pillar 3  Community-based financial services  We will improve access to financial services through the development of networks of non-bank agents, electronic money and digital finance. The National Payment Processor (PRONAP) project, which is scheduled to go into production in mid-January 2017, is in line with this objective. Pillar 4  Consumer Education and Protection  this involves creating and implementing a framework for the promotion of financial education and consumer protection in Haiti. Pillar 5  Strengthening Institutions and Infrastructure  We will support the strengthening and consolidation of savings and credit cooperatives and micro institutions non-mutual finance, implement a legal framework for the insurance sector, and strengthen financial and supporting infrastructure, including biometric identification and urban and rural land securitization. Ladies and gentlemen, however, the challenges ahead are enormous Apart from the implementation of ongoing reforms, Haiti's national financial inclusion strategy, in order to achieve the BRH's vision, must address the following challenges: 1. It shall assist users and providers of financial services in solving: or The irregular and low incomes of some poor households and MSMEs, resulting in smaller (and also more expensive) transactions and a need for financial products and services that can help manage risks and smooth consumption; or Low levels of formal education and literacy that impede the ability of Haiti's population to understand and use formal financial services; or The absence of a legal and regulatory framework for the protection of consumers of financial services; or The high level of informality of the Haitian economy, in particular, MSMEs, which can impede their ability to access financial services, especially loans; or The inability of many Haitians to have identity document, and appropriate collateral for loans, particularly in rural areas. According to UNHCR, 1.82 million Haitians do not have an official identification document and, according to some estimates, one million Haitians do not have birth certificates. This limits their ability to complete any transaction with a financial institution, including opening accounts (beyond basic e-wallet accounts); or The problem of the authenticity of title deeds, which discourages greater use of land as collateral, thus blocking viable investments and limiting the demand for credit. 2. In addition, the financial inclusion strategy should help establish an appropriate framework for the development of economically sustainable networks of non-bank agents that offer all types of financial services from official providers in urban, suburban and rural areas that do not have branches of financial institutions. Considering developments in other countries where non-bank agents have contributed significantly to increasing the availability of financial products and services offered by banks and other official entities, regulations are being revised to allow these financial institutions to mobilize agents to provide all kinds of financial services beyond those already offered, such as, for example, allowing customers to access their account held with banks and/or credit unions, allowing customers to open bank accounts and apply for loans, making international money transfers, subscribing to microinsurance products, etc. In the near future, such a network of agents will have to be interoperable in order to increase its viability and intensify competition between the different providers. 3. It will also help to: or Diversify financial products, especially those geared towards low-income people (e.g. with no-frills accounts), MSMEs (e.g. through leasing and microinsurance products) and farmers (e.g. through insurance products); or Address the relative high cost of certain financial services, including international remittances; or Strengthen the operations of sustainable financial service providers oriented towards low-income households and MSMEs (mainly savings and credit cooperatives and microfinance institutions), and enable them to achieve economies of scale, take advantage of information and communication technologies in order to diversify their services, and increase their effectiveness; or Influence, strengthen and improve the impact of public and private sector efforts to combat poverty, improve the health and education level of vulnerable groups, promote agricultural production and increase the efficiency and production of high value-added MSMEs for the national economy. However, the use of digital financial services by previously excluded customers not only brings benefits, but also creates various types of new and changing risks. Like what:  Digital Transaction Platform Risk: Pooling funds and entrusting the storage and management of account balances of different customers to a third party will create risks related to the real-time accuracy and reconciliation of the data of a troubled account holder to that of the account managing entity.  Digital Technology Risks: The quality and reliability of digital technology affects the risk of service disruption and loss of data, including payment instructions;  Agent Risks. Agents and their networks introduce new operational risks, risks of financial crimes and risks associated with consumer credit, risk of fraud, theft of money and database, risk of contravening the rules on the fight against money laundering and the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT); To mitigate these new and evolving risks, the Central Bank will need to adjust its supervisory and regulatory regimes. Over the past five years, banks and mobile phone companies have increasingly sought to capture new market share and become increasingly active in digital financial inclusion.  For banks we can mention: Soge izi, Unibank all Kote and lajan cash of the BNC;  for the Digicel: mon cash and Tcho Tcho mobile Access is only a first step towards financial inclusion. We want everyone to be able to become full players in the financial system and not just consumers of this digital economy. We want everyone from the simplest grower to the most sophisticated entrepreneurs to become contributors to this digital economy and the development of our country. For everyone to truly benefit from this digital economy, we must manage to reduce the production gap that is very often linked to the level of learning, the challenges of illiteracy and the lack of infrastructure. But I remain convinced that if each of us does our part, we will be able to make this journey through the digital economy towards a fairer and more inclusive Haitian society. Thank you.

Title: Speech on October 5, 2016 at the Caribbean Central American Action (CCAA) forum in Washington DC on the theme: Future of Banking in the Caribbean Basin
text: Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois on October 5, 2016 at the forum of the organization "Caribbean Central American Action" (CCAA) in Washington DC on the theme: Future of Banking in the Caribbean Basin" Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois on October 5, 2016 at the Caribbean Central American Action (CCAA) forum in Washington DC on the theme: Future of Banking in the Caribbean Basin Introduction Just as many Caribbean countries, Haiti is facing new challenges with the phenomenon of De-risking. International financial institutions have been exiting relationships and closing accounts of clients perceived to be high risk. International banks that have pulled out have referred to recommendations of The Financial Action Task Force (FATF) as the main reason for taking de-risking decisions. By doing so they have effectively denied and/or restricted entire classes of customers from financial services without conducting a comprehensive assessment of the actual level of risk and without considering adopting risk mitigation measures to keep these customers. Financial institutions in Haiti like many in the Caribbean have made continuous efforts to identify, assess and understand the risks of money laundering and terrorism financing to which they are exposed and take measures to commensurate to those risks in order to mitigate them effectively. The banks have worked towards compliance to the Know Your Customer (KYC) policy and to ensure that all clients fill when appropriate the declaration of source of funds. At the Central Bank and at the Government level, we have focused mostly on how to decrease country risk by accelerating implementation of GAFIC recommendations. However as many other countries have learnt now, it is not sufficient to avoid the disengagement of correspondent banks. Nonetheless we continue to strengthen our regulations. This past month we had parliament approved legislation on AML/CFT and on our financial intelligence unit, UCREF. The Government has gone as far as cancelling the creation of an offshore banking center to avoid additional compliance concerns for the financial sector. The scope of the impact of de-risking is very large and its damaging impact is wide spread including negative effects on growth and on financial inclusion. Haitian financial system and its current correspondent banking relationships Haitis financial sector has several institutions involved directly or indirectly in a correspondent-banking relationships. They include: 7 domestic banks, 4 money transfer operators (two domestic and two international) and, more than 100 credit unions institutions Over the past three years, many domestic financial institutions have lost ties with three US correspondent-banks. From those that still maintain relationships with domestic Haitian banks, one has put restriction on letters of credit and check clearing transactions. Today, only two Haitian domestic banks are able to offer to their clients these services. Two US banks have ended their relationships with one domestic Money transfer Operator. However the financial system is still able to do international financial transactions, but, the de-risking phenomenon affected relationships especially with correspondent banks in the US. This is most worrisome because the USA is the country with which Haiti does the majority of its trade and most remittances come from there. Remittances in Haiti yearly represent about 20% of GDP and plays a crucial role in poverty reduction. In Haitis we do have some relationships with correspondent banks in Canada, France and the United Kingdom. However, Haiti mainly relies on US correspondent banks for international transactions. The situation is fragile since only three US banks constitute the core of correspondent banking relationships for the Haitian financial system and among those only one is offering international financial transactions to four out of the seven Haitian domestic banks. De-risking and Remittances In Haiti, these transfers from migrant workers have been very stable and have even registered upward trend in recent years. Since 2000, these flows have become greater than exports earnings and international aid. They compensate largely the goods and services deficit to represent 20% of our GDP in 2015. They finance mostly basic consumption needs such as food, school and health expenditures. Incoming transfers in Haiti amounted 2.2 billions of dollars in 2015 and 75% of these remittances are from the USA. The loss of correspondent banking relations will have a major impact on the Haitian economy and will be very damaging for the poorer and most vulnerable families since remittances are sometimes the only source of income for many of them. In addition that de-risking will affect remittances in many other ways: We may observe an Increase in the cost of sending remittances if some international operators withdraw from the circuit). We may not be able to avoid an expansion of the informal sector. The withdrawal of legally registered players could encourage the use of pocket transfers. Hence, rather than reducing risk in the financial sector, de-risking in fact may cause an increase in vulnerability by pushing high-risk clients to smaller financial institutions that dont have enough AML/CFT capacity. Hence, instead of de-risking there could be a situation of re-risking because of lack of controls. We may also observe an increase of financial exclusion which may roll back progress achieved thus far towards financial inclusion goals. De-risking and trade finance Banks play an important role in trade finance and correspondent banking relationships are very allow international trade to take place by facilitating cross border payments. In Haiti, banks are pivotal for international trade, especially for imports. And any decision that may affect the service offered by these intermediaries can only have negative consequences for consumers. Total trade of goods accounted for 53.7 % of GDP in 2015 and 74.3% for goods and services for the same year. In 2015, 93% of Haitis total export were destined to the USA and 60% of all Haitis foreign exchange outflows for international trades and other individual needs were destined to the USA. Some other effects of De-risking On Trade 1. Increase in the informal sector (no longer use regular channels (banking), importers must use less safe channels to supply the market). 2. Possibility of increase in smuggling, financial transactions underground (reduction in custom and fiscal revenue) 3.-Loss of credit card settlement services On FDI De-risking is also very threatening to foreign direct investments in the particular case of Haiti where it may result in the delocalization of existing foreign investments and render it impossible to attract new investments. Conclusion I am very pleased to witness that intense attention is being given to the issue of de-risking. We are hoping that this dialogue, the workshops, conferences and meetings will lead to tangible and concerted solutions. The violent hurricane Mathew that just shook the country, left many homeless and several tens of thousands of others without a source of income or means of livelihood. Remittances I am sure will play a critical role. Imagine one minute if money transfers could not be made to Haiti.

Title: Speech on the occasion of the conference debate on remittances to Haiti and their impact on the national economy
text: Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois on the occasion of the conference debate on remittances to Haiti and their impact on the national economy Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois on the occasion of the conference debate on remittances to Haiti and their impact on the national economy Ladies and Gentlemen, Dear Participants, It is a pleasure to participate in this conference-debate on "remittances to Haiti and their impacts on the national economy". I thank the General Coordinator of the Council for Economic and Social Development of the Prime Minister's Office, Mr. Louis Naud Pierre, for his invitation, which I accepted all the more eagerly as the subject is of importance for the central bank. I hope that this symposium  with this line-up of distinguished analysts and high-level experts such as Charles Castel, my predecessor at the BRH, Fritz Duroseau my current colleague on the Board of Directors, and other academic and international specialists  will lead to fruitful exchanges that can lead to public policies conducive to economic stability and growth. Ladies and Gentlemen, It is difficult to exaggerate  at least for Haiti  the importance of remittances, commonly referred to as unrequited transfers of funds from abroad or current transfers in the international balance of payments nomenclature. This aggregate, which includes official donations received from abroad and remittances from workers of Haitian origin, amounted to US 2.5 billion (26.1% of GDP) billion in 2014, including US 563.0 million in official donations and US 2.0 billion (19.7% of GDP) in workers' remittances. Current transfers (on a net basis) are expected to reach US 2.7 billion per year (29.2% of GDP) and workers' remittances around US 2.3 billion (25.0% of GDP) from this year to the 2020-2021 fiscal year. At 22.7% of GDP in 2014, Haiti is in 8th place in the list of the largest recipients of transfers (or the countries most dependent on workers' remittances) after Tajikistan, Kyrgyz Republic, Nepal, Tonga, Moldova, Liberia and Bermuda, according to the World Bank. Ladies and Gentlemen, Current transfers are not "produced" by the economy like exports of goods and services and do not depend on the economy like imports of goods and services. Net export earnings come from real counterpart activities while current fund transfers It is a relatively autonomous aggregate compared to the rest of the country. In fact, there would be a negative relationship between the state of the economy and current transfers to the extent that humanitarian aid and workers' remittances increase significantly after natural disasters, ceteris paribus. Pending further studies on the subject, remittances seem to depend much more on the income of sending countries than on the action of receiving countries. Thus economic stagnation, degradation of the physical environment and population explosion, favoring the massive  often illegal  emigration of Haitian nationals to North America and the Caribbean (and now to South America) coincide with an extraordinary expansion of current transfers from US 64.8 million in 1981 to US 234.3 million in 1991 to reach US 768.6 million in 2001 and US 2.8 billion in 2011. A first observation is that current transfers, while financing the rest of the economy, are growing faster than GDP and, therefore, do not contribute much to growth. A second observation that derives from the first: apart from the construction of residences and the acquisition of agricultural implements and other tools of production, remittances, particularly workers' remittances, increasingly finance imports of food or clothing, to the detriment of local production. A third observation is the dynamism observed in outward transfers (as opposed to outward transfers), particularly since the earthquake of January 2010. Reinforcing a trend that dates back to the late 1980s, with the university turbulence and the relative deterioration in the quality of education, outward transfers permanently finance the schooling of members of emigrant families, often from secondary level. Ladies and gentlemen, The BRH is responsible for preparing the balance of payments and, therefore, compiles data on current transfers of remittances, including workers' remittances, both to and from outside. It works jointly with its partners including IHSI, the Center for Latin American Monetary Studies (CEMLA), the IDB and the IMF to constantly improve the quality of statistical data. The BRH also closely monitors transfer flows for the purpose of systematically assessing liquidity in the foreign exchange and money markets, as part of the execution of monetary policy. Remittances in the form of remittances have become the largest source of external financing in the Caribbean and Africa, far outpacing official development assistance, direct investment and portfolio investment. The recent World Bank report predicts that workers' remittances will exceed US 500.0 billion per year over the next few years. But, in addition to the magnitude of these flows, it has been observed that remittances "have an intrinsic value in terms of development" and play a role of "vector to facilitate greater financial inclusion", according to the International Organization of La Francophonie. Transfer income supports daily consumption of food and energy as well as basic investments in education, for example. These resources also finance the start-up of many small and medium-sized enterprises and are also "an important tool for improving women's economic empowerment... . In this context, BRH is working hard to achieve the global target of reducing transfer costs by 11-5%, access to remittance services for the poorest and using transfers to facilitate greater financial inclusion and quality economic growth. With that, ladies and gentlemen, I wish the conference every success. Thank you. Port-au-Prince, 28 March 2017

A 22.7% du PIB en 2014, Hati figure en 8me place dans la liste des plus gros receveurs de transferts (ou les pays les plus dpendants des envois de travailleurs) aprs le Tadjikistan, la Rpublique Kyrgyz, le Npal, Tonga, la Moldavie, le Libria et les Bermudes, selon la Banque Mondiale.
