En fait, il y aurait une relation ngative entre ltat de lconomie et les transferts courants dans la mesure o laide humanitaire ainsi que les envois de travailleurs augmentent sensiblement aprs les catastrophes naturelles, ceteris paribus. En attendant plus dtudes sur le sujet, les transferts de fonds semblent dpendre beaucoup plus du revenu des pays expditeurs que de laction des pays receveurs. Ainsi la stagnation conomique, la dgradation de l environnement physique et l explosion dmographique, en favorisant l migration massive souvent illgale-de ressortissants hatiens vers l Amrique du Nord et les Carabes (et maintenant vers lAmrique du Sud) concident avec une expansion extraordinaire des transferts courants de US $64.8 millions en 1981  US $234.3 millions en 1991 pour atteindre US $768.6 millions en 2001 et US $2.8 milliards en 2011. Un premier constat est que les transferts courants, tout en finanant le reste de lconomie, augmentent plus vite que le PIB et, par consquent, ne contribuent pas beaucoup  la croissance. Un deuxime constat qui drive du premier :  part la construction de rsidences et lacquisition dinstrument aratoires et dautres outils de production, les transferts de fonds, particulirement les envois de travailleurs, financent de plus en plus plus les importations de produits alimentaires ou dhabillement, au dtriment de la production locale. Un troisime constat est le dynamisme observ des transferts vers lextrieur (par opposition aux transferts de lextrieur) notamment depuis le tremblement de terre de janvier 2010. Renforant une tendance qui remonte  la fin des annes 1980, avec les turbulences universitaires et la dgradation relative de la qualit de lenseignement, des transferts vers lextrieur financent en permanence la scolarit des membres de familles migrs, souvent depuis le niveau secondaire. Mesdames, Messieurs, La BRH a la charge de la prparation de la balance des paiements et, par consquent, compile les donnes sur les transferts courants de fonds, notamment les envois des travailleurs, aussi bien vers que de lextrieur. Elle travaille conjointement avec ses partenaires notamment l IHSI, le Centre dEtudes Montaires Latino-Amricains (CEMLA), la BID et le FMI pour lamlioration constante de la qualit des donnes statistiques. La BRH galement surveille de prs les flux de transferts  des fins dvaluation systmatique des liquidits sur le march des changes et le march montaire, dans le cadre de lexcution de la politique montaire. Les transferts sous forme denvois de travailleurs sont devenus la plus grande source de financement extrieur dans les Carabes et en Afrique, dpassant de loin laide officielle au dveloppement, les investissements directs et les investissements de portefeuille. Le rcent rapport de la Banque Mondiale prvoit que les envois de travailleurs dpasseront US $500.0 milliards lan au cours des prochaines annes. Mais, outre lampleur de ces flux, il a t observ que les transferts de fonds  possdent une valeur intrinsque en matire de dveloppement  et jouent un rle de  vecteur pour faciliter la plus grande inclusion financire , selon lOrganisation Internationale de la Francophonie. Les revenus de transferts supportent la consommation journalire en nourriture et en nergie ainsi que les investissements de base dans lducation, par exemple. Ces ressources permettent galement de financer le lancement de bon nombre de petites et moyennes entreprises et reprsentent galement  un important outil damlioration de lautonomisation conomique des femmes . Dans ce contexte, la BRH met tout en uvre pour la ralisation de lobjectif mondial de rduction des cots des transferts de 11  5%, laccs aux services de transferts pour les plus pauvres et l utilisation des transferts pour faciliter une plus grande inclusion financire et une croissance conomique de qualit. Sur ce, Mesdames et Messieurs, je souhaite le plus grand succs  la confrence. Merci. Port-au-Prince, le 28 mars 2017

Title: Speech on the occasion of the cocktail of the 7th International Summit on Finance
text: Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois on the occasion of the cocktail of the 7th International Summit on Finance Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois on the occasion of the cocktail of the 7th International Summit on Finance CEOs and Representatives of Commercial Banks Distinguished representatives of the private sector Mr. CEO of the Growth Group Mr. CEO of PROFIN Dear colleagues of the BRH Board Ladies and Gentlemen The International Summit on Finance has become the most popular annual event for practitioners of economic and financial issues as well as for academics seeking a space for structuring reflections on financing development in Haiti. The forum, it is true, has taken on a major dimension in recent years with the great diversity and utilitarian nature of the activities developed in the workshops. The second edition of Fin Tech, which is held in the continuity of a successful initiative that began last year, attests to the good health of a Summit that is now well established and has acquired its letters of nobility. This year again, the menu is plentiful but balanced. A difficult arbitration but always within the reach of efficient organizers who are not at their first attempt. The activities are of the highest quality, which guarantees the satisfaction of this august assembly that you form and the critical minds that you represent. The richness of the International Finance Summit is there; in this melting pot of ideas and diversities. Welcome to the 7th edition. The central theme is of utmost importance: Financing Real Estate in Haiti. It is at the heart of a broader issue: the need for strong and sustained growth in the face of intense demographic dynamics. Ladies and gentlemen I would like to be complicit in an act of contagion tonight. That of communicating to you the joy and enthusiasm that I feel to deliver this address on the occasion of the 7th edition of the International Summit on Finance and the second edition of the Fin Tech. But I don't just speak for myself. I speaks on behalf of the Growth Group and its Chairman and CEO Kesner Pharel to whom I address a warm tribute for the quality of organization and regularity of an event that grows each year in terms of participation and the relevance of themes of major interest for public policies and economic actors. I speaks on behalf of the many stake holders whose quality and level of representation attest to the interest of a growing community in financial issues and development finance in general. I certainly speaks on behalf of the Bank of the Republic of Haiti, which in recent years has moved to the other side of the scenes to become an active co-organizer of the Summit. Our team is working hard to improve the added value that our institution brings to the organization of the event. It thus guarantees the objective of familiarizing economic actors more with the vision, objectives, instruments of the Central Bank as well as the constraints it faces. So you understand why the success that will cover the meetings held during the five working days of this Finance Week will not be the result of chance. A significant number of actors will have contributed to this. Also, allow me to associate the voice of the august assembly that you represent with that of the Board of Directors of the BRH to address warm thanks to all those who, natural or legal persons, at one level or another, have made this 7th edition another success. Ladies and gentlemen The problem of development remains the major theme in a country, where in 65% of cases, the Gross Domestic Product per capita is negative over the last 36 years. As a central banker, financing growth under sound macroeconomic conditions is at the heart of this issue. It is therefore a question of excluding the extremes of euphoria of haste and paralysis of wait-and-see. From this point of view, the consolidation of financial institutions, their development and the broadening of their spectrum of action represent the appropriate path to a reasoned approach to monetary policy that supports growth. The National Strategy for Financial Inclusion is part of this process and our strengthened presence at this Summit responds to the need to promote it through one of the important pillars of this strategy: financial education. Thus, during the past week and throughout the week devoted to Finance, BRH executives are visiting public and private secondary schools to expose students in the final classes to basic elements in economics and finance and to deal with topics related to the mission and activities of the Bank of the Republic of Haiti. Financial education is a long-term endeavour that will have to reach all segments of the population. However, it is expected to bear fruit fairly quickly and the expectation of its socio-economic return is among the highest. For a Policy Maker, nothing beats a population educated about economic issues and informed about the policies implemented. This is the primary guarantee for the emergence of a double predictability: that of the response of economic agents to the measures envisaged and that of the solutions that decision-makers must provide to the problems raised. This constitutes the royal road to the primacy of rules in the conduct of public policies without omitting the role that this information plays in the formation of expectations. Such an approach should benefit both the single framework of the macroeconomic environment and the multiple sectoral policy frameworks. And in the case that concerns us today, to the success of an enlightened policy of financing the real estate sector. This sector is at the junction of three dimensions of sustainable and integrated development. It is an important sub-branch of the Buildings and Public Works branch around which the economic and social infrastructures are built. It is an indicator of social mobility and strengthening of the middle classes. It is a perennial component of the engine of economic growth through significant direct effects and renewed induced effects. These are essentially the motivations of the Central Bank in promoting this sector. Ladies and gentlemen The housing deficit is a structural problem that some experts point to the period of independence. It is part of a broader situation linked to the problems of housing and urbanization without excluding it from the overall problem of spatial planning. However, the nature of the problem requires a joint approach based on medium- and long-term considerations. It follows that the answers to the problems of housing cannot wait for the long period of implementation of a comprehensive urbanization policy. It must, however, take them into account to ensure the sustainability of investments in the field and reduce the future expropriation costs that urban modernization will impose on households and the Treasury. The Central Bank's reflections and provisions in favor of financing the real estate sector date back well before January 12, 2010. The oldest of these provisions dates from the law (decree) creating the Savings and Housing Banks which exempts them from 50% of the minimum reserves in force. This attests to a strong tradition of concern of the institution for the financing of the real estate sector which accumulated, in 2009, a housing supply deficit of 300,000 units out of a stock of occupied housing of the order of 2.1 million units according to estimates from combined sources. The earthquake has greatly widened the already very serious supply deficit. The estimates, however, fall within too wide a range to be consistent. They range from a minimum of 105,000 to a maximum of 300,000 units destroyed. Fortunately, an authoritative statistic, since coming from the Haitian state, estimated in 2013, that "the metropolitan area of Port-au-Prince alone will require at least 500,000 additional housing units over the next 10 years to fill the pre-earthquake deficit, to repair the damage of the earthquake and to meet the substantial demand for housing resulting from urban development. " Today, we can only approach the issue of housing in Haiti in terms of a deep crisis. But deep as it is, this crisis contains the seeds of renewal. It will depend on the leadership of public authorities and the insight of private investors to take advantage of it. The nature of the real estate problem makes it a sector with very high growth potential. These are not just housing units to be built. From a modern perspective: this is a field whose profile and content remain to be designed; it is an economic area whose social significance is essential if we want to reconstitute the middle classes; It is a sector that easily lends itself to a broad dynamic of wealth creation thanks to the multiplicity of value chains it induces and the sustainability of the process it can trigger. Conducting an all-out policy for the development of the real estate sector is therefore a necessity from a social point of view and a necessary step from an economic point of view. A consequent undertaking that will aim to repair a centuries-old drama that finds its manifestations in a scattered rural habitat and an anarchic expansion of urban spaces. The Central Bank is working to find the best means, in terms of arrangements and financial mechanisms, to amplify its contribution to the implementation of a project that remains a major objective of growth and development. Its role remains anchored in the (economic) dimensions of this major project: One Incentive contribution to the creation by the private business sector of a diversified supply of housing and buildings under the best conditions of costs and physical environment The promotion of a growth dynamic likely to guarantee the solvency of a steadily increasing demand that allows a sufficiently high profitability to sustain the sector The effort to mobilize resources to finance the heavy investments required to achieve economies of scale beneficial to the market. I will forgive you for boring financial calculations that do not necessarily fit my address. But let us at least attempt a simple arithmetic of the real estate question. Let's stay in line with a study made public after the earthquake of 2010 to stick to an annual demand of 4500 to 5000 units from the middle class. Under reasonable conditions of economy of scale, an average unit price of 75,000 is in the order of possible transactions for standard level housing. For this middle class component alone, we are achieving an annual level of about 350 million in residential investment. Resources within the reach of the formal financial system and whose cost of borrowing would not exceed 700 a month to tend towards 350 at the end of a mortgage of 20 years with interest subsidized in the order of 5% to 6%. I will not go further in inference to project the direct and ripple effects of such an investment effort on the economy. Let us simply admit that they are potentially important and sustainable if they are renewed over a medium-term horizon. But the steps, you would say, to make feasible objectives of this magnitude, in the context of the development of the real estate sector, are multiple and are due to strong structural, legal and institutional constraints. The major constraints of the cadastral problem that limit the implementation of a housing policy, ration real estate financing while increasing costs. The multiplicity of administrative and fiscal costs, the cumulation of which weighs on the share of financial resources responsible for the real estate establishment itself. The inadequacy of an outdated legal framework that causes serious capital costs on the mortgage portfolio of financial institutions due to too long delays in the realization of properties pledged as collateral. These problems, to name but a few, are part of an overall failing environment that discourages investment in the sector and dilutes the impacts of incentives for its financing. Hence the fundamental role that public policies are called upon to play in loosening the constraints of a field of production capable of driving growth and animating various sectors of economic activity. The implementing decree of the law on co-ownership is a step in the right direction. It encourages the modernization of a sector whose full potential requires two courses of action: That relating to the constraints of a structural nature and of a legal-administrative nature to create a framework of sufficient attraction and profitability of the Investments. That aimed at reducing over the medium term the import component of construction costs in order to magnify the indirect effects induced by the growth of the sector. In terms of resource mobilization, the Central Bank is continuing the work necessary to align its action with the development requirements of the real estate sector. Particular emphasis is placed on the contours of the financial environment capable of supporting the financing effort that will have to mobilize all the players in the banking system and beyond. We are aware of the limitations of a partial approach where cost concerns outweigh the coordination of public policies from diverse backgrounds. This is why our reflections focus primarily on sequencing policy actions that will shorten the time taken to achieve the objectives sought. Meanwhile, the policy of stimulating credit for the rehabilitation of the housing sector is ongoing. As you know, the BRH has taken measures to exempt from minimum reserves the resources collected by banks and used for credit purposes for housing and the hotel sector. Similarly, memoranda of understanding have been signed with certain banks as part of a programme to finance, on favourable terms, the acquisition, renovation or construction of housing for the benefit of creditworthy customers. The real estate market's responses to these provisions will expand as structural and institutional constraints such as the cadastre are flattened. To circumvent this last problem, the BRH has embarked on reflections to orient a part of its housing policy towards the financing of promoters or developers of large real estate projects for the benefit of public service executives, professionals and the Haitian diaspora. These projects should include the construction of apartment complexes for rental or sale in condominiums, the construction of residential villages, and the acquisition and servicing of land for a housing project. This program, once launched, should serve as a basis for the development, in the medium term, of a bond market through the securitization of mortgage portfolios. The establishment of such a market could contribute to a better allocation of the savings of economic agents, thus fueling a virtuous circle of development of this sector of the future. Ladies and Gentlemen I hope I have communicated to you some of my enthusiasm on the real estate issue. At the beginning I pointed out that the path of solutions to the problem of the sector is not that of extremes: no rush... or wait-and-see. The response to the earthquake of 12 January 2010 was a good example of this measured behaviour. The BRH identified measures that focused on the cost and accessibility of housing credit. An approach that, at first, necessarily fell within the framework of a partial approach. For both the debtor and a creditor, this sense of urgency could only be answered in monetary policy instruments to ease tensions in the real estate market and invite economic agents to be more optimistic. With the benefit of hindsight, a more comprehensive approach was required to reflect on the issue of real estate. It makes it possible to integrate a better understanding of the pre- and post-earthquake dimensions into emerging solutions. In recent years, the reflections have gone through a process of maturation that can be found in the quality of the proposals and the character of application that emerges from them. The 7th Finance Summit is the ideal space to record these proposals in a coherent framework of reflections for action. Financial practitioners, policy makers, industry professionals, academics and investors will benefit. That's the whole point of this enthusiasm that I want to be contagious. It is therefore with emphasis that, on behalf of the Board of Directors of the Bank of the Republic of Haiti, I thank all those who make this Summit the success it already is. These thanks go particularly to the Growth Group team and its CEO Kesner Pharel as well as to the BRH team who worked under the supervision of a member of the Board of Directors in the person of Ronald Gabriel. May they find here the expression of our gratitude. Thank you!

Title: Speech at the Workshop on Good Corporate Governance  Organized by the International Finance Corporation (World Bank) and the Bank of the Republic of Haiti (BRH)
text: Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois  Workshop on Good Corporate Governance  Organized by the International Finance Corporation (World Bank) and the Bank of the Republic of Haiti (BRH) Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois  Workshop on Good Corporate Governance  Organized by the International Finance Corporation (World Bank) and the Bank of the Republic of Haiti (BRH) Honourable Parliamentarians, Mr. Secretary General of the Prime Minister's Office, Mr. President of the Superior Court of Auditors and Administrative Litigation, Ladies and Gentlemen Members of the Government, Madam Resident Representative of the World Bank, Mr. Representative of the International Monetary Fund, Mr. Resident Representative of IFC, Representatives of International Organizations, Ladies and Gentlemen, Mayors of the metropolitan area, Ladies and Gentlemen Directors General, Ladies and Gentlemen Representatives of the Public Administration, Dear Colleagues of the Board of Directors, Ladies and Gentlemen, Distinguished Guests, On behalf of the Board of Directors of the Bank of the Republic of Haiti, I would first like to wish and express my warmest thanks to all the personalities who kindly responded to our invitation to this workshop, to discuss the theme: "Governance", which reflects your interest in moving things forward. My words of thanks also go to all those who supported the organization of such a workshop, we mean the World Bank Group. Let me first set some context for this workshop. The reflection on good governance is part of institutional capacity building and especially the will of leaders to make this issue the linchpin of a modern and effective state. The current economic and social environment, particularly characterized by: a significant deterioration in household living standards, a rise in the prices of basic consumer products, a recurrence of natural disasters and external shocks multiplies the challenges facing the central State. Despite the efforts made and carried out within the various public institutions and local authorities, the issue of governance is significant for the State. If the debates on corporate governance, synonymous with the art of better governance, date back to the 30s, this concept is still being sought in Haiti and the holding of this workshop reflects our concerns. Manage economic, public and private affairs through known institutions, mechanisms and procedures, efficiently and equitably for the well-being of individuals and communities. That is a definition of good governance. Haiti's development requires the strengthening of the state and the adoption of good practices in governance. This requires a strong political commitment on the part of the authorities, who must make them explicit and provide the necessary means for their success. We are convinced that strengthening good practices in the governance of Haitian institutions will contribute more effectively to improving their performance and, therefore, to the economic development of our country. Institutional capacity-building is therefore necessary. Ladies and gentlemen Governance refers to the rules, practices and norms observed in the management of a country. Good governance respects the values of transparency and ethics and complies with the legal requirements in force in the country concerned. Sound and transparent governance therefore requires rigorous practices, including regular accountability. It also aims to combat corruption, which in essence circumvents and distorts established rules. The rules also call for everyone's responsibility, starting with leaders at the highest level, including Boards of Directors and, to some extent, General Management. Therefore, it is important that steps be taken to ensure that a national policy is in place that will require close collaboration among several stakeholder groups, each with a set of key roles and responsibilities. Ladies and gentlemen It is time to align our visions of economic and social development. The production of wealth and the creation of jobs are priority conditions for sustaining the reforms already initiated and for supporting a sustainable economic recovery. Thus, the mobilization of resources and the efforts that are being made can only be fully successful with a policy of good governance. I would like to conclude by inviting you to make better use of this workshop to strengthen governance arrangements within your respective structures. Thank you

Title: Remarks on the occasion of the 1st International Summit of Digital Women in Haiti  Chamber of Commerce of Women Entrepreneurs of Haiti  "ICTs, New Opportunities for Women's Empowerment and Inclusive Growth"
text: Remarks by Mr. Jean Baden Dubois, Governor of BRH, on the occasion of the 1st International Summit of Digital Women in Haiti  Chamber of Commerce of Women Entrepreneurs of Haiti  "ICT, New Opportunities for Women's Empowerment and Inclusive Growth" Remarks by Mr. Jean Baden Dubois, Governor of BRH, on the occasion of the 1st International Digital Women Summit in Haiti  Chamber of Commerce of Women Entrepreneurs of Haiti  "ICTs, New Opportunities for Women's Empowerment and Inclusive Growth" Mrs. Daniella Jacques, President of the Chamber of Commerce of Women Entrepreneurs of Haiti. Ladies and gentlemen, in your ranks, ranks and qualifications. It is with pleasure that I address you today on the occasion of this symposium, which addresses a very important theme: that of strengthening the role of women entrepreneurs. If there is one thing that is the subject of the broadest consensus in Haiti, and in the global spheres related to economic development, it is that of the crucial role played by women entrepreneurs in the structure and successful functioning of various economic and social processes throughout the world. Despite the still strong dominance of the patriarchal heritage, women's productive and income-generating contributions remain highly visible and, without doubt, vital in more ways than one. The sustainable prosperity of nations now seems virtually impossible if women are excluded from market and productive mechanisms, or if restrictions are imposed on their access to available resources. This is why, since the end of the 20th century, the Gender and Development approach has focused on gender relations to both promote economic and social development and pursue sustained poverty reduction. Nowadays, the concept of sustainable development can only be conceived from a gender perspective, which requires not only a vision of integration of the fundamental rights of all, but also the systematic pursuit of equitable and non-discriminatory policies, particularly with regard to gender. This gender perspective now flourishes through a notion that the English language defines as gender mainstreaming, i.e. the search for gender equality. Such a concept advocates that the effort to implement any development programme should be based on the development of gender issues, as well as on the promotion of human rights. We must agree on one essential point. Working to ensure that women have a frontline place in the economic development agenda is not only a humanitarian impulse, nor simply a concern to redress a universal historical injustice. Contemporary societies have no alternative but to give women a prominent place on the economic agenda because women are indispensable for such an agenda. There is countless empirical research, which demonstrates the much greater economic success of societies that treat men and women more equitably. Nations that have made the opposite choice have experienced lower economic growth, as well as limited capacity to reduce poverty. Similarly, gender-based social disparities have historically produced inefficient economic outcomes. For example, an analysis published in 2003 by a World Bank task force estimated that if, between 1960 and 1992, African countries had reduced the gender gap in school enrolment at the same rate as East Asian countries, the result would have been a doubling of per capita income in the African region over the three decades. Indeed, women's reputation for reliability and credibility has made them the preferred workforce in the transnational textile and electronics industries. Already microfinance programs around the world, and certainly here in Haiti, have shown a preferential option for women because they have proven to be good financial managers who are second to none in repaying loans with discipline, according to the agreed schedule. The argument that women should be placed at the centre of economic development is also justified by women's proven ability to be a more judicious distributor of goods and services within the home. With regard to our country, specifically, the reputation of women as a vanguard economic agent is well established. The image of the merchant carrying her basket of provisions on her head, or holding food stalls in public markets, has become symbolic, very characteristic of informal economic activity, the majority in Haiti. The marketing of a large part of rural production goes through the "Madan Sara", this emblematic entrepreneur whose business successes are sometimes miraculous. It is not without reason that it is often referred to to characterize the Haitian economy. Many of these women, often part of a very small business, manage to provide for their children and make them first-rate professionals. N'hessitons pas a le last: woman z bones rel economics and society of Haiti. Therefore, our women, many of whom are Vanyan fanm, must be offered a better operating environment than the one that currently exists, and which is characterised by such limitations as follows: insecurity, low profitability, the marginalization as an informal sector not always well regarded, and and so on. It is necessary to work a? better development and organization of women's activities, especially in the agricultural world where their dynamism makes them play a leverage role. Such an approach cannot do without the entrepreneurial approach. Women's entrepreneurship is one of the best strategies to enhance the socio-economic status of women, to stop them from being second-class economic agents confined to informal economic activities. In a perspective of economic decentralization and wealth creation in a context of sustainable development and poverty reduction, the use of technology seems a first-rate solution. In the specific case of women entrepreneurs, it is a question of taking advantage of the many opportunities offered by new information and communication technologies (NICTs) in terms of improving the performance of companies in general. Consideration should be given to how to use tools such as smartphones, tablets, etc., as well as software such as marketplace applications or cloud applications, to take advantage of the efficiency opportunities offered by the technologies in question. In the long term, new information and communication technologies make it possible to exploit the potential of a company, to structure the information system, to gain in performance and productivity, and to take advantage of the latest innovations. In addition, thanks to the Internet, the company opens up to the world and can make itself known. The face of entrepreneurship is changing and evolving thanks to technology that makes it easier to create market share, and also to make the most of potential and talent. Obviously, achieving this goal of prosperity and productivity is not easy, and women entrepreneurs will have to overcome many obstacles and constraints. They will face many challenges such as: the problems of lack of financial inclusion; and also the inadequacies of legislation concerning the computer world, electronic commerce and other related fields; and and deficiencies in financial education that prevent optimal decisions to be made in terms of the choice of financial services or ways to better deliver services It is all the more desirable to consider a new path for women entrepreneurs in Haiti as their current situation is very difficult. Unable to meet the requirements of formal financial institutions, women entrepreneurs often resort to informal financial channels, such as loans granted by relatives, by a "notable" of the region or by a usurer; "soil", etc. Microcredit granted by microfinance institutions is also widely used by women entrepreneurs for small amounts, those of less than 100 thousand gourdes. It is enormous, the work that awaits us all, including the Haitian State. For its part, the BRH is resolutely committed to a financial inclusion strategy aimed at protecting both the consumer and the producer. We want to pay special attention to women entrepreneurs to facilitate their access to credit and other financial services. In doing so, we are seriously considering this objective of the national strategy paper, which provides for the promotion of the use of new information and communication technologies (NICTs) for the provision of financial services. Through the various actions to be implemented, the ultimate objective is to open the financial market to women entrepreneurs through NICTs and regulations adapted to their needs while taking into account the country's structural obstacles. Let us therefore combine our strengths and resources to enable our women entrepreneurs to fully access the place that their extraordinary contribution to the daily functioning of the entire Haitian community has always earned them. I therefore wish you all a fruitful colloquium. Jean Baden Dubois Governor

Title: Speech at the opening of the Finance Session of the Haitian-American Business Summit (HABS) organized by the Haitian-American Chamber of Commerce of Florida (HACCOF) Miami, Fl
text: Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois at the opening of the Finance Session of the Haitian-American Business Summit (HABS) organized by the Haitian-American Chamber of Commerce of Florida (HACCOF) Miami, Fl Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois at the opening of the Finance Session of the Haitian-American Business Summit (HABS) organized by the Haitian-American Chamber of Commerce of Florida (HACCOF) Miami, Fl Minister of Haitians Living Abroad, Stephanie Auguste, Minister of Tourism Gessy Menos, Miami-Dade Commissioner Monestime, Director General of the CFI, Dear Members of the Board of Directors of the Bank of the Republic of Haiti, Ladies and Gentlemen Elected Representatives of the Diaspora, Members of the Board of Directors of the Haitian-American Chamber of Commerce of Florida (HACCOF), Distinguished guests, dear colleagues, It is an honor for us at the Bank of the Republic of Haiti to participate in the Finance Session of the Haitian-American Business Summit organized by HACCOF. I welcome the participation of the President of the Republic. I see in the participation of the Head of State in this important event a manifestation of his will often expressed to facilitate the transformative role that the mobilization of resources, capacities and networks of the Diaspora can enable it to play in the development of our country. I also welcome the support of the Speakers of both chambers of the Haitian Parliament, which is part of the desire to help unleash, between Haiti's business sectors and those of the Diaspora and America, synergies capable of facilitating the development of the many potentials that the Haitian economy holds. In this regard, it is also worth mentioning the presence at this Summit of personalities working in the financial and investment communities of Haiti and the Diaspora. I thank the President of the Haitian-American Chamber of Commerce of Florida for inviting the BRH to speak at today's meeting. Our acceptance of this invitation is placed in the overall context of the efforts that the BRH has been making for some time to intensify its use of the means at its disposal as an institution of the Haitian State charged by its organic law with conducting Haiti's monetary policy and ensuring the stability of the national financial system. This mission, the importance of which cannot be overemphasized, requires the BRH to remain constantly mobilized in order to play, in a timely and appropriate manner, its role in the establishment and maintenance of the conditions necessary for the smooth functioning of the national economy. In carrying out this mandate, the BRH is doing its best to provide frank and effective collaboration with the other state bodies involved, some of them on the front line, in the essential work of designing actions and policies that can help achieve the same fundamental mission. In addition to public sector partners, BRH also remains constantly attentive to opportunities for fruitful collaboration that may come from private sector partners, both from within the country and from our vital Diaspora. Yes, I mean our vital Diaspora. Statistics show that in 2000, Haiti was already among the countries in the region sending the highest number of highly skilled workers. To quote Ponce, in his overview of South-South migration and Haiti's development, "For the year 2004, 35% of Haitian doctors left Haiti for the United States, Canada, Australia and the United Kingdom. In sum, it is estimated that 80% of Haitians with a university degree (bachelor's, master's or doctorate) do not live in Haiti. So 80% of the Haitian intelligentsia is in the diaspora... Please, my dear friends and compatriots, do not leave it to only 20% of the Haitian intelligentsia to develop and save our dear Haiti that we say is our homeland. We need the financial capital that is the diaspora, but we need your well-trained and experienced human capital even more. Our acceptance of HACCOF's invitation is therefore placed in this general context. We see our participation in this Business Summit as containing a triple potential, as a carrier of an opportunity for information, collaboration and promotion. In the first place, the presence of the BRH at working sessions held by compatriots of the Diaspora outside Haiti is exceptional enough for me to take the opportunity to share with the participants useful information, which can help to put us in tune with regard to the general evolution of the Haitian economic reality. Such information will help shed light on Haiti's macroeconomic framework in order to highlight the conditions conducive to maximizing viable business opportunities in promising economic sectors. On the other hand, I anticipate that this Business Summit will promote the discovery, at various levels, of multiple affinities and modalities of collaboration. On the basis of the information provided and the experiences already acquired on the ground in Haiti, these affinities and modalities should allow our sisters and brothers in the Diaspora, and also foreign investors, to take a much greater interest in Haiti's latent capacities, which are just waiting to be fruitful. It is therefore a question of working on the deployment of the potential of capacity building. From this point of view, it is to be hoped that the milestones laid during this Summit will be seeds that, if sown wisely, will generate projects that will maximize the investment windfalls that abound in our country. Hence the opportunity for promotion contained in this Summit. Provided that the right efforts are made to ensure follow-up, this meeting should help project a more coherent image of our country to foreign investors, particularly Americans, who would come to appreciate the viable business opportunities offered by promising economic sectors in our country. Distinguished guests, dear colleagues, My intervention will focus on the following four (4) axes: 1. First, I will provide an overview of our country's macroeconomic framework over the past thirty-five (35) years. It will be a question of shedding a constructive light on the challenges facing us all, in order to be well imbued with the efforts that lie ahead. 2. Then, I will recall the potential for investments existing within the Haitian economy, a potential that is intended as many business opportunities for the Diaspora. This is all the more the case since an unparalleled level of private transfers, and also other contributions, already makes the Diaspora the pillar of the Haitian economy, an invaluable reservoir of investments capable of stimulating capacity building. 3. Third, I will analyze some examples of successful investment projects in Haiti. This will show that, in our country, there is no shortage of business opportunities for investors from the Diaspora, nor for that matter for foreign investors. 4. Finally, I will conclude with the presentation of the incentive mechanisms put in place by the central bank in support of productive sectors with high potential. Let us therefore address the first axis, which concerns a quick overview of Haiti's macroeconomic framework, seen through the following (3) observation elements: 1. From 1981 to 2016, the country's economy grew at an average rate of about 0.5% per year, and episodes of inflation of varying degrees of high inflation, especially during the periods 1992-1994 and 2003-2004. 2. The efforts made in recent years have led to an improvement in economic performance. Such efforts must be stepped up in order to counteract the persistent effects of certain imbalances, including that of the external account, maintained by the shortcomings of exports compared to imports; and also the imbalance of public finances, fuelled by insufficient tax revenues. For our country, progress is urgently needed, which is also justified by the need to counter hazards such as changes in the socio-political situation, the damage caused by natural disasters and the negative impact of external shocks such as the sharp increases in oil prices that occurred for years and until the beginning of the current decade. It should be noted that many of these increases were absorbed by the Treasury, whose resources did not have the necessary depth to assume such a burden on a sustainable basis. 3. The stabilization programmes put in place periodically by the Haitian authorities have made it possible to limit the deleterious impact of these imbalances and uncertainties. However, the great challenge for all of us remains to do everything possible, and on all fronts, to accelerate the pace of growth so as to achieve a significant improvement in the purchasing power and living conditions of the population in the long term. Dear compatriots of the Diaspora, Haiti's economic challenge is daunting, but the problems are not insurmountable. We must not give up. For its part, if the BRH is clearly aware of the challenges facing our country, it is to signal the urgency of getting to work without delay and redoubling its efforts to meet these challenges, once and for all. In this perspective, the Central Bank of Haiti is simply an institution at the service of the progress of our country, with a view to an inclusive Haiti. It sees itself as a link in a large national chain, a partner among many, ready to bring a frank collaboration to any development effort in accordance with its statutory attributions. And this idea gives me the opportunity to move on to the second axis of this presentation, to recall both the good prospects of the Haitian economy, and the place that must play this indispensable partner that is the Diaspora. As I said earlier, and it is worth emphasizing, our economy is full of investment opportunities. Moreover, its performance has improved recently, as indicated by the following indicators: 1. The average annual growth rate of the economy has hovered around 2% over the past 5 years, and a more robust result is expected for the 2017-2018 fiscal year. 2. In the current fiscal year (2016-2017), net foreign exchange reserves increased by approximately US94 million, reaching US1.022 billion as at 24 May 2017. 3. Compared to September 2016, the gourde appreciated by 4.1% in May 2017 against the US dollar. 4. Monetary financing of the fiscal deficit was more than halved in the period from FY2015 to FY2016. It thus increased from 9.9 billion gourdes on September 30, 2015, to 4.5 billion gourdes on September 30, 2016. The improvement in the public finance situation should continue, on the one hand, with the maintenance of the cash management agreement established between the Ministry of Economy and Finance and the BRH and, on the other hand, with the gradual decrease in the significant subsidies granted by the Haitian State on the purchase of petroleum products. It should be noted that the strategy of cash management is to pursue effective management, i.e. without waste or excess, of the government's cash flows and short-term cash balances. Such a financial management posture generally applies both within the government itself and between the government and entities with which it reports. It is worth noting that this favourable development in the recent macroeconomic situation that we have just reported is not unrelated to the holding of presidential and legislative elections and the establishment of a new Government in a relatively short period of time. However, the multiple effects of Hurricane Matthew have not yet dissipated, especially in terms of squeezing local food supply and soaring prices of products thus rarefied by this new natural disaster. Nevertheless, the central bank's planned interventions in the foreign exchange market should, in conjunction with other measures by both the BRH and the state authorities, help contain inflationary pressures. It should be noted that these interventions provide for foreign exchange sales of 120 million over the remaining half of the 2016-2017 fiscal year. More generally, the current measures are more likely to succeed in the long term with the implementation of an economic recovery strategy based on the gradual orientation of these measures towards the consumption of locally produced goods and services, rather than the consumption of imported products. Such a strategy should be based on strengthening our institutions, reducing market imperfections and minimising the major structural constraints on our economy. That said, what are the prospects offered today by the Haitian economy? What role can our compatriots living abroad play in the implementation of such perspectives, especially given their proven commitment to supporting their homeland? Let us first consider the question of the role of the Diaspora, both historical and future. Numerous empirical studies have demonstrated the direct and indirect positive effects of private transfers on the balance of payments and on growth. The effects of transfers can be observed on savings and investment, but also in physical and human capital formation, and again through the increase in consumption and the reduction in the volatility of growth. A study published under the auspices of the World Bank in 2003 considers that the level of consumption in rural areas can have a multiplier effect within the economy, as the recipients of transfers direct their spending towards local products, instead of imported products. The financial contribution of the Diaspora is among the largest capital flows to Haiti, with an upward trend since the mid-1990s and a clear acceleration from 2010. It should be noted that remittances from the Diaspora have a more constant relative weight than agriculture in gross domestic product, or GDP, and a higher weight than that of development aid. Haiti is the third largest recipient of remittances in the Caribbean. Remittances from our Diaspora increased on average from 5% of GDP during the period 1992-1996, to more than 23% of GDP over the period 2011-2016. Meanwhile, the contribution of transfers to financing Haiti's trade deficit increased on average from 27% to 70%. In 2015, these transfers exceeded the flow of foreign direct investment by a multiple of 20, and were at a level close to that of remittances from the Dominican Republic's Diaspora. Since the early 2000s, remittances from Haitians living abroad have become the main component of Haiti's foreign exchange supply. Beyond this very important financial contribution, the Diaspora provides Haiti with considerable potential in terms of increased productivity, human capital formation and the development of the housing sector. Indeed, according to a study published by the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB), education represents, after food, the second largest item in the expenditure of transfer recipients. The survey highlights that the contribution of the Diaspora is equally significant in the housing sector. For example, the informal sector devotes a significant share of the transfer amounts received from abroad to residential construction. Distinguished guests, dear colleagues, The uniqueness of the weight that the Diaspora has come to give itself in the economic reality of our country, is indisputable. Since the theme of investment is at the heart of this summit, it seems appropriate to raise the following question. If most of the remittances from the Diaspora were no longer destined for consumption, as is currently the case; if the Diaspora came to accept the idea, all in all reasonable, that good business and investment opportunities are not lacking in our country; If, therefore, a growing number of Haitians living abroad decided to invest funds in Haiti that they intended to invest elsewhere, then, one may ask, what would happen to the contribution of the Diaspora to the sustainable development of the Haitian economy? Of course, and assuming the validation of the three premises I have just mentioned, it is difficult to assess now the extent of the increase that would occur, in the future, in the overall level of Diaspora investment in Haiti. However, in the absence of a credible assessment, it is reasonable to assume a sustained increase over time in the business initiatives of Haitians living abroad. And it is precisely this process of sustained increase in its investments in Haiti that the BRH wishes, today, to urge the Diaspora to trigger. Hence the last two points of my speech. First, to convince the owners of capital in the Diaspora that the idea of investing in Haiti is not utopian, I would like to submit to your spirit of examination some examples of success in terms of investments in the country. Next, I will describe measures developed by the BRH as incentives for the productive sector and exports. In the case of local investments, quality financial packages have made it possible to integrate the contribution of partners from the Haitian Diaspora into the capital of local companies. These arrangements were carried out in three key sectors of the economy: the food industry, hotels and energy production. With regard to foreign direct investment, or FDI, two aspects must be considered: financial arrangements and the integration of local production into value chains, as in the case of the National Brewery, or Brana, and that of the small millet. We are talking about success stories that have been achieved in the food industry and with companies operating in the mobile phone sector and hotel establishments operating within the framework of an international franchise. It should be noted that foreign direct investment reflects a long-term interest in the destination country, and it has the advantage of being low volatility, unlike portfolio investment. Their impact on employment, the tax base and economic growth is more stable. In addition, FDI is often accompanied by contributions of new know-how, new technologies, and new production and management techniques. They therefore contribute to enriching their sectors of activity by making them more productive and competitive, and by facilitating their access to international markets, often through the networks of companies to which FDI belongs. As an illustration, let's take the hotel business, which nowadays is part of networks made up of travel agencies (real or virtual), cruise agencies, airlines, insurance services, etc. It is therefore imperative to work to establish the virtuous circle that will lead to the emergence of other success stories through the development of a framework where public investment will fully play its role as a catalyst for private investment, especially that of the Diaspora. This is all the more urgent as the country now faces a dual reality. On the one hand, private domestic savings in Haiti are very low compared to the enormous financing needs involved in sustainable development and significant poverty reduction. The Haitian financial system has only about 1.4 billion in resources that could, when circumstances permit, be directed towards viable promising projects with a reasonable level of risk. On the other hand, investment funding from PetroCaribe funds has been reduced to almost one-fifth of what it was about three years ago. Indeed, the available PetroCaribe funds have increased from nearly 15 billion gourdes in 2013, or nearly 4% of GDP, to 3 billion gourdes in 2016, or 0.65% of GDP. As for the call for external savings, which combines official grants, public loans and private loans, it remains conditional on the requirements of multilateral financing agencies and the availability made possible by the economic performance of bilateral donors. It is therefore necessary to minimize certain structural and institutional constraints in order to provide direct access to private savings and, hence, to work towards the deepening of the financial market. For example, access to international capital could be promoted through the pooling of local and Diaspora resources and through the development of international guarantee instruments and other risk mitigation mechanisms. It is therefore desirable not only to seek complementarity between available savings and unrequited private transfers, but also to consider new solutions to stimulate investment in Haiti. There is no need to emphasize, once again, that in the pursuit of such an objective, the quest for the fullest engagement of the Diaspora must remain a major goal. It is therefore in this perspective that the BRH has implemented specific programmes to promote certain key productive sectors with high added value, which could have a direct impact on employment and economic growth. These programmes to encourage the productive sector, which aim to facilitate credit to the private sector, are as follows: 1. The KAY PAM program, set up after the earthquake of January 12, 2010 to stimulate housing credit for the middle class. It has the following characteristics: the interest rate is between 8% and 10%, and it is fixed over 10 years; The financing is denominated in gourdes, and it covers the construction, renovation and acquisition of houses. 2. The Free Trade Zone Development Program, established in December 2015, focuses on increasing the country's ability to benefit from the HOPE II* and HELP** Acts, which were renewed by the U.S. Senate in August 2015 for 10 years. Created in partnership with commercial banks, this program not only increases exports and the number of jobs in the textile sector, but also allows free zone promoters to obtain financing from banks on favorable terms including a maximum interest rate of 7%. 3. The export financing program established following memoranda of understanding signed in October 2016 by BRH with two development finance companies, the Industrial Development Fund (FDI) and the Haitian Industrial Financial Corporation for Economic and Social Development (SOFHIDES). This program promotes access to credit for enterprises producing goods and services for export. It includes a window for refinancing accounts receivable from exporters, and a credit facility to strengthen the productive capacities of targeted enterprises. This should lead in the medium to long term to the reduction of the balance of payments deficit. 4. The Tourism and Hotel Incentive Programme, whereby banks are exempted from the requirement to set up minimum reserves on the resources they use to finance projects in the tourism and hospitality sectors. These sectors can thus obtain credit at more favourable interest rates. Other projects are under consideration as part of incentives for productive sectors. These include, in particular, the promotion of real estate development projects; the promotion of co-ownership and agricultural free zones; and the introduction of partial credit guarantees and insurance programmes for the agricultural sector. Finally, the BRH has recently embarked on a series of activities to facilitate dialogue and reflection between key players in different sectors of activity with high added value. This exercise aims to strengthen policies and financing mechanisms capable of influencing the country's economic development in a sustainable manner. Dear friends, The effectiveness of all the measures I have just summarized goes hand in hand with the support of the State through structural reforms aimed at improving the business climate in Haiti. However, it is undeniable that business opportunities already exist in the country. The example of the success of local and multinational companies, which, without mentioning them by name, I have just mentioned provides evidence of this. Having chosen to invest in Haiti, most of them have already taken their place among the country's largest taxpayers. I therefore invite compatriots living abroad to follow the examples of these predecessors using the formulas that have proven their effectiveness. The Diaspora has every interest in taking advantage of this. Its contribution to the development of its homeland would rise to an otherwise important level if it complemented its traditional transfers with investment-oriented initiatives in Haiti. Regional and local associations of the Diaspora could join forces with the Haitian authorities, particularly municipalities, in a logic of public/private partnership intended to finance regional development projects. Investment needs and opportunities are immense in basic socio-economic infrastructure such as education, health, drinking water distribution and renewable energy. The Diaspora could also invest directly in companies that agree to open their capital. The aim would be to promote the expansion or creation of semi-public enterprises within the framework of joint operations with institutions already involved in this type of activity, such as the Industrial Development Fund (IDF) and the International Finance Corporation (IFC). Finally, in addition to the creation of regional chambers of commerce and the establishment of business networks, the contribution of the Diaspora can also extend to trade exchanges and the transfer of skills and technology. Ladies and gentlemen, these are some initiatives that could gradually reduce the obstacles to investment in Haiti, and transform the vicious circle in which we find ourselves, into a virtuous cycle of strong and sustained growth, and continuous substantial improvement in the standard of living of the population. The Bank of the Republic of Haiti plays its part through pro-growth measures to promote the productive and export sector. It will continue to oversee the financial system through appropriate regulation and supervision. I am confident that the discussions that will follow will be of high quality, and I express the hope that the work of this Summit will be crowned with success. Jean Baden Dubois Governor of the Bank of the Republic of Haiti

Title: Speech at the launch of the forum on the issue of currency availability and distribution in Haiti
text: Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois at the launch of the forum on the issue of currency availability and distribution in Haiti Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois at the launch of the forum on the issue of currency availability and distribution in Haiti Madam Director General, Representatives of the Ministry of Economy and Finance, Mr. CEO of the Growth Group Ladies and Gentlemen Directors of Commercial Banks, Distinguished representatives of supermarkets and other commercial establishments, Dear colleagues from BRH and the banking system, Distinguished guests, On behalf of the Board of Directors of the Bank of the Republic of Haiti, BRH, and on my own behalf, I warmly welcome you to this Forum dedicated to the "Issue of the distribution and availability of currency in Haiti". The theme of today's forum is of an importance that cannot be overemphasized. This importance stems from the vital nature of money in any society that participates in the movements and transactions of the modern economy. It is true that, for some time now, traditional money has been plagued by vigorous competition from various non-physical forms of medium of exchange. It is also true that the most marked monetary evolution denotes a growing trend towards dematerialization, especially with the recent emergence of electronic currencies such as bitcoin. However, this reality still does not prevent physical money or cash from remaining the necessary element for full exchange in our contemporary production societies. In fact, there has been no hesitation in attributing to the movement of circulation of money within the economy attributes similar to the movement of blood through the human body. Such a preponderant role, even essential one might say, is explained by the fact that money is an intermediary of choice which allows economic agents to manifest an effective demand for the various products available on the market. It is therefore this unique instrument for improving trade circuits, an essential link in the economic chain that unites production and consumption. It is a function that money has always exercised, and this, as numismatics reveals to us, through the various forms it has known since barter from the very beginning. Even more fundamentally, and from a conceptual point of view, money enables market operators to quantitatively assess that demand in order, on the one hand, to express its strength in relation to available supply and, on the other hand, to reflect the relative scarcity of goods and services as expressed by the price system. To this must be added the instrumental assets of money, which are manifested through its various functions. Thus, the currency: herself is a unit of account, by its divisibility ; she is a store of value, due to its durability; and It becomes a means of payment, by the collective consensus that guarantees its invariable acceptability. Therefore, in view of all the issues arising from the role it assumes in financing the economy, it is understandable that money is at the heart of the Central Bank's implementation of its mission to monitor the functioning of the financial system in order to ensure its constant stability. This is because cash remains, until today, the predominant means of settling routine financial transactions in the domestic economy. As a result, it is up to the Central Bank to ensure that the Haitian economic system, in all its components, without exclusion, has a reliable currency, and available without restriction and continuously. This mandate consisting in ensuring that the means of payment in fiat currency made available to the public are sufficient to meet the needs of the economy, is entrusted to its Direction de la Caisse et du Reseau that the BRH has entrusted it. Such a mandate is in direct line with the vision that the Board of Directors that I have the honour to lead has defined for BRH, and I quote: "A modern and efficient central bank, concerned about price stability and the development of the financial system and determined to encourage the growth of real sectors of the economy with a view to an inclusive Haiti." End of quote. However, the BRH believes that a system can only function at its point when there is consistency between the behaviours of all the structures that compose it. If one component fulfills the role of another, confusion will be created, bottlenecks will form, and inefficiencies will develop. Naturally, this system will eventually run out of steam. The organization of this Forum stems both from this vision of inclusion of the real sectors of the economy and from this mandate to ensure the adequate supply of fiat money to the market. Various topics will be debated during the day. These include: the the need to create a mechanism for dialogue between the Banks' Chief Operating Officers in order to better serve economic agents; the the problem of the availability of money in our country; the announcements and proposals to be made by the Management of the Fund and the Network for a more modern and efficient management of cash management issues; and and so on. All these conversations and exchanges are part of this policy of openness that the BRH intends to practice with regard to all actors in the real economy. The holding of this Forum is also one of the many manifestations of our policy of sharing and disclosing financial information. By welcoming you here this morning on the occasion of the launch of this Forum, I hope to testify, if it were necessary, to the importance that the current Board of Directors of the BRH attaches to the stability of our country's financial system. It is also a pledge of support for the management of the Caisse and the Network, which has resolutely embraced the Board's vision and which, in recent times, has distinguished itself by a number of initiatives geared towards the modernity and efficiency that we advocate. I am thinking in particular of the acquisition and commissioning of sophisticated equipment such as the CPS 1500, intended for automated ticket counting, or the BDS, which will be used to destroy mutilated banknotes. I therefore encourage you to participate actively in the exchanges and debates in order to enable us to find realistic and lasting solutions to the various problems that concern us, in the hope of reaching a consensus, a "modus operandi" for the harmonious functioning of the system. Have a great day, and good work everyone! Jean Baden Dubois Governor of the BRH

Ds lors, au vu de tous les enjeux qui dcoulent du rle quelle assume pour le nancement de lconomie, lon comprend que la monnaie se place au cur de la mise en uvre par la Banque Centrale de sa mission de surveillance du fonctionnement du systme nancier en vue den assurer la stabilit constante. Ce mandat consistant  sassurer que les moyens de paiement en monnaie duciaire mis  la disposition du public susent pour rpondre aux besoins de lconomie, cest  sa Direction de la Caisse et du Rseau que la BRH la confie. Un tel mandat se place en ligne directe de la vision que le Conseil dAdministration que jai lhonneur de diriger a dfinie pour la BRH, et je cite :  Une banque centrale moderne et eciente, soucieuse de la stabilit des prix et du dveloppement du systme nancier et dtermine  encourager la croissance des secteurs rels de lconomie dans loptique dune Hati inclusive . Title: Speech at the Forum on Co-ownership
text: Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois at the Forum on Co-ownership Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois at the Forum on Co-ownership Mr. Minister of Economy and Finance, Honourable Parliamentarians, Madam, Mayors, Ladies and Gentlemen Directors General, Ladies and Gentlemen representatives of the banking and financial system, On behalf of the Board of Directors of the Bank of the Republic of Haiti and on my own behalf, I warmly welcome you to this forum dedicated to the economic issues of co-ownership. Ladies and gentlemen In Haiti, residential space is becoming increasingly scarce while the population is constantly increasing. The increasing urbanization of our departmental capitals and the capital requires new territorial development and sustainable development plans. The occupation of the space of cities must be thought and rethought in a more functional way if we take into account the existing. Vertical development is the only way to deal with the housing problem. Socio-economic, cultural and environmental impacts will of course have to be taken into account. At the legal level, the law of 13 August 1984 organizing the co-ownership regime and the decree of 15 December 2011 laying down the procedure and modalities of application of the law of 13 August 1984 constitute the basic legal framework. In addition, in 2013, the real estate sector was declared a priority under the provisions of the Investment Code in support of the national housing promotion policy. To this end, incentive benefits have been granted to eligible companies. Despite this device, which could be described as embryonic, there is not really a major real estate project to see the light of day in the country. Admittedly, social housing and apartment construction projects have been initiated in the last twenty years. However, these initiatives have shown their limit with the scarcity of residential spaces. In addition, the BRH, while pursuing a generally restrictive monetary policy to combat gourde volatility and inflation, has set up and strengthened several programs aimed at facilitating the financing of certain key productive sectors with high added value and which can have a strong influence on the quantity of jobs created and on economic growth, This is done in collaboration with financial institutions. Thus, since 2011, the BRH, in tandem with most of the banks in the market, has been implementing with some success, a residential real estate refinancing program to stimulate bank credit for housing, fill the housing deficit and facilitate access to homeownership. The idea is essentially to act on the availability of credit, reduce the financial costs of borrowed funds and make real estate loans more attractive for individuals and financial institutions. The program, called Kay Pa'm, has helped banks finance residential construction with: one interest rate that varies between 8 to 10% one fixed interest rate over 10 years, and one financing exclusively in gourdes. The success of the Kay Pa'm program has resulted in an increase in the number of participating institutions and mortgage products available to clients. The latest data suggest a significant increase in residential real estate loans, following the expansion of this program. However, this is far from enough. From combined sources, it was estimated that there was a housing supply deficit of 300,000 units in 2009 out of a housing stock of 2.1 million occupied units. The 2010 earthquake further widened this deficit. A statistic from the Haitian state estimated in 2013 that "the metropolitan area of Port-au-Prince alone will require at least 500,000 additional housing units over the next 10 years to fill the pre-earthquake deficit, repair earthquake damage and meet the substantial demand for housing following urban development." Ladies and gentlemen The housing problem in Haiti remains worrying. However, it is necessary to analyze, discuss, exchange and pose problems: what are the public policies in terms of urbanization and housing? We must raise the problem of the cadastre, the problems linked to the environment. We need to address real estate financing issues and the risks faced by financial institutions, without ruling out the legal aspects, the registration of securities and contracts, taxation and, finally, explore avenues such as the possibilities of partnership between the State and the private sector. Economic support for the construction sector cannot be adequately provided if these issues are not addressed and viable solutions are not found and implemented. However, the advantages of co-ownership are multiple. It is irrational to think that this housing deficit can be filled with our traditional way of building isolated residences, one by one....... The condominium meets a need because of its convenience and its generally more affordable acquisition cost. Condominiums can address the shortage of decent housing for middle-income households under better conditions of cost and physical environment. It is therefore essential to raise awareness among public and private actors, to inform real estate developers, businessmen and women, bankers and other economic operators of this significant opportunity available to them, but obviously still too little known to the general public. The BRH is engaged in reflections to orient part of its policy towards a refinancing program of Real Estate Developers, or developers of large real estate projects for the benefit of public service executives, professionals and the Haitian diaspora. These projects should focus on the construction of Apartment Complexes for rental or sale in co-ownership, the construction of residential villages, the acquisition and servicing of land for a housing project. Once launched, these programs should serve as a basis for the development, in the medium term, of a bond market through the securitization of mortgage portfolios. We hope that this forum will make it possible to better identify the constraints, to highlight the difficulties, to provide avenues for reflection and to lead to public housing policies, the strengthening of the building sector, the enhancement of trades related to construction, a concise and adequate legal framework, the development of financial mechanisms, to increase real estate credit, but above all to make decent housing accessible to households and families. This, ladies and gentlemen, is a real challenge for the country's economic development. To begin to face this challenge, this forum offers us the opportunity to carry out an in-depth reflection for the construction of condominiums with a view to reducing costs and risks. We thank the distinguished panelists who accepted our invitation today and wish the Forum every success. Thank you! Port-au-Prince, 29 June 2017
