Title: Speech on the occasion of the 1st decade of the Fdration Le Levier
text: Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois on the occasion of the 1st decade of the Federation Le Levier Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois on the occasion of the 1st decade of the Federation Le Levier Members of the Board of Directors, Ladies and Gentlemen, I am honoured to take part today on behalf of the BRH Board of Directors in the celebration of the first decade of the Federation Le Levier. The constitution of this federation represents an important shift in the development of the cooperative sector and its consolidation. From its birth to today, the Bank of the Republic of Haiti has been able to observe the significant progress of the federation despite the difficulties and obstacles encountered. My presence here today demonstrates BRH's desire to fully play its role as regulator not only of the banking system, but of the entire financial system. The Board of Directors is betting heavily on the cooperative sector to confirm the opportunities to be seized from an inclusive perspective. The creation of the federation has also enabled the BRH to strengthen ties with the cooperative sector through certain projects that aim to ensure the viability of savings and credit cooperatives. Ladies and Gentlemen, The modernization and stability of the sector remains the main objective of the BRH. The common thread of BRH's action is the primacy of the collective interest and the economic and social development of those who do not have access to the traditional banking system. For this, the success of the sector requires that the federation be viable, solid and comply with laws and regulations while motivating its member caisses in terms of training and accompanying them for sustained growth. Dear leaders of the Federation and Savings and Credit Cooperatives, In order to harmonize practices and communicate more effectively and efficiently, the BRH wishes to strengthen the existing links between the two institutions. The BRH wants the cooperative federation model to be more than a group of caisses populaires, but also to be a channel working to promote financial inclusion for the benefit of all, especially the most modest. The logic of cooperatives is not only part of the initiation of sustainable activities, but also in the conduct and organization of the sector. We want to see better-managed and more prosperous credit unions, we want to see credit unions achieve returns on investment in the same order of magnitude as their peers in the banking system... Among the actions carried out by the BRH to promote internal economic growth, financial inclusion occupies an important place. A large number of people in Haiti operate outside the financial system and are therefore deprived of financial services. This leads economically to great inequality even though we are all equal before the law. As a regulator of the financial system, BRH is keen to facilitate the match between supply and demand to ensure access to financial services and products for the population and thus provide them with adapted services and products. To achieve this, the role of cooperatives, and in particular of the federation, is preponderant. By offering its services to individuals and SMEs, the cooperative sector plays an important role in having a positive impact on finance accessible to all and serving as a major strategic tool for decision-makers. Thus, the BRH has combined its efforts to provide the federation with some financial instruments to pave the way for change and modernization of the CECs. The SPIH, the Clearing House, the CEC Modernization Project and the Bureau of Credit Information (BIC) are all tools that are boosting the sector to an enviable level. The federation must equip itself with adequate means and the necessary infrastructure to better expand its operations and satisfy its members in a dynamic, competitive and demanding environment. The BRH urges you to arm yourself with rudiments to make the institutions you style more and more seasoned. The BRH, aware of the issues and challenges facing the financial and economic landscape, encourages the philosophy of federation in favor of increased efficiency in the conduct of cooperative governance. Moreover, the financial instruments promoted by the BRH send a powerful message in the repositioning and future of cooperatives. My determination to the sector as Governor has remained intact. So, needless to say, Le Levier is called upon to play a crucial role with regard to the national strategy for financial inclusion. At this pivotal moment in our life as a people when the economic and financial map of the globe has been redefined; where the difficulties of our country challenge us; Where the very foundations of our social pact are wavering, more than ever the federation must mobilize all its members to share, to work in order to make the sector more dynamic and more concerned about the economic development of members. In closing, I hope that several more decades will follow this first, which we are celebrating today. Happy birthday.

Title: Speech at the Conference on the Economic Transformation of Grand'Anse
text: Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois at the Conference on the Economic Transformation of Grand'Anse I must begin by congratulating the President and members of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Grand'Anse for this initiative to organize, in partnership with the Bank of the Republic of Haiti (BRH), this conference on the economic transformation of this geographical department. I offer my heartfelt thanks to the organizers for this great honor done to the BRH by associating it with this activity which coincides with the patronal feast of Jeremiah, the magnificent city of poets. I therefore take this opportunity to wish, on behalf of my colleagues on the Board of Directors of the BRH and on my own behalf, a happy birthday to all Jeremians. It is therefore a great pleasure for me to speak at this prestigious event, which will undoubtedly help to highlight the many economic potentials of the Grand'Anse department. The department must recover from the adverse consequences of Hurricane Matthew by creating a favourable climate for private investment. Since the earthquake of January 12, 2010, the BRH has been trying to play its part in the recovery of the national economy through mechanisms to stimulate productive credit, that is to say, with high added value and with induced effects on economic growth, exports and the creation of sustainable jobs. Under my administration, within a public policy framework described as "pro-growth", these mechanisms initiated in the real estate sector have been strengthened and extended to other economic sectors, including Agriculture and Agribusiness. It is therefore in this particular context that I will talk to you about the objectives of these mechanisms. The BRH, through its organic law, intends to use the means at its disposal to conduct Haiti's monetary policy and ensure the stability of the national financial system. By carrying out this mandate, it ensures that its actions are part of the recovery framework defined by the government authorities. I always look forward to participating in these meetings, which provide an opportunity to exchange ideas, debate and share reflections with a view not only to helping macroeconomic stability, but also to contributing to robust and sustainable growth. Like that of other regions of the country, the population of Grand'Anselaise, estimated in 2015, at about 468,000 inhabitants, is young and looking for opportunities. Public policies have so far failed to produce the level of collective well-being to which it aspires and is entitled. We want, through these incentive mechanisms, articulated with other public programs, to give it the chance to work, to undertake, in order to reduce its dependence on private transfers from our sisters and brothers in the diaspora. We also see in our participation an opportunity to assess, at the level of Grand'Anse, the lack of information that prevails throughout the national financial system and that affects the efficient allocation of savings to viable investments. BRH intends to make every effort to make available information on its policies, the measures adopted and the projects on which it is working. With this in mind, a new Communication Department has been created to improve the information circuit with the general public at the national level. Therefore, I give you the guarantee that Grand'Anse will not be left behind in this process. Without wishing to awaken painful memories that made us all suffer after the passage of Hurricane Matthew, I must still say that these events were for me an opportunity to appreciate the courage and sense of solidarity of the Grand'Anselaise population. Allow me to salute the resilience of this population which, despite disasters and dramatic situations, has always been able to rise to build and rebuild. Like a Phoenix, this population knows how to rise from the ashes. People who know how to build cannot disappear. It is this thinking that motivates people to invest and make a bet on the future. My dear friends We are in a region that, throughout history, has always been? Considered one of the main granaries in the country, especially for quality? of its fruits (coffee?, cocoa and real tree), for diversity? of its tubers and for the abundance of its coasts in seafood. Many of the ideas contained in this plan are still relevant and can serve as a basis for reflection in the implementation of a plan to boost investment in the region. Based on the natural capacities and other potential of the region, it is in my humble opinion possible to trigger the growth dynamic necessary to improve living standards. You just have to want it and believe it. Food imports are on the rise. In 1986-1987, they accounted for 19.2% of total imports. This ratio rose to 27.7% in 2014-2015. I say, for the wrong reasons, because this decline in the weight of agriculture is not attributable to an increase in that of the processing industries, but to an increased dependence on the outside. To be effective, it is essential that public investment adequately fulfills its role as a catalyst for private investment. The latter, which generally reflect a lasting interest on the part of the project promoter in the target country, have several virtues. Our net foreign direct investment flows have never historically exceeded 200 million per year, while for the Dominican Republic and South Korea, they reached 2.5 billion and 10.8 billion respectively in 2016. Ladies and gentlemen As entrepreneurs, producers and entrepreneurs, you are well aware of the importance of credit in the development of economic activity and the link between credit, investment, production and employment. However, you will agree with me that increasing credit to the private sector does not automatically lead to economic growth and lower unemployment. Recall that in 2014-2015 the credit granted by the banking system increased by nearly 20% after having increased by an average of 30% during the fiscal years 2010-2011 to 2012-2013, while the economic growth rate was only 1.4% for a population growth of 1.8%. This credit growth has to a large extent favoured imports of consumer goods at the expense of local production. The level of poverty therefore increased slightly during this period. It is in this particular context that we welcome any effort by the authorities to improve the quality of public investment, improve the coherence of public policies and minimize structural obstacles to production, investment and exports. Haiti's financial system is highly liquid. He is waiting for this to direct his idle resources towards promising projects capable of changing, in a lasting way, the destiny of our Haitian brothers and sisters. It is therefore with this in mind that the BRH has implemented specific programmes to promote certain key productive sectors with high added value and potential, which could have a direct impact on employment and economic growth. These incentive programs, which will be presented to you later, allow for expanded access to credit in local currency and on affordable terms. In particular, they aim to: 1. Increasing housing supply and falling rents as well as reducing construction costs and improving urbanization; 2. Stimulating the assembly sector and exports and associated jobs as well as increasing the number of industrial spaces available in the country; 3. Stimulating exports in general, local production and net foreign exchange earnings from the economy; 4. The development of the tourism sector, mainly through its hotel component; These sectors can thus obtain credit at more favourable interest rates. Other projects are under consideration as part of incentives for productive sectors. These include, in particular, the promotion of real estate development projects; the promotion of co-ownership and agricultural free zones; and the introduction of partial credit guarantees for the agricultural sector. The BRH encourages all actors involved in the development of agriculture to set up insurance mechanisms, especially for crops. The latter must play a key role in mitigating the many risks to which the sector is exposed and which too often make the cost of credit dissuasive in the eyes of debtors. Finally, the BRH has recently engaged in a series of activities to facilitate dialogue and reflection between key players in different sectors of activity with high added value through sectoral consultation tables. The latest, organized by the Ministry of Agriculture, focused on the cocoa sector. This exercise is based on the identification of the obstacles characterizing the different links in the value chain and which initiate its evolution. It also covers the development of recommendations to the competent authority for the minimization of the identified brakes. It therefore aims to strengthen policies and mechanisms that will promote increased funding for projects that are increasingly viable and capable of influencing the country's economic development in a sustainable way. BRH has come to you to share this useful information. She is confident that they will be put to good use. It is by laying these milestones that we will succeed in creating in the department of Grand'Anse, this virtuous circle that should induce: improving the production and exports of goods and services, including tourism services; some sustained and sustainable job creation; one increased productivity of labour and capital; one broadening the tax base; one sustained increase in GDP per capita; one expanding the middle class; the Projection of a new international image of the department and the country in the eyes of potential investors and consumers. Thank you for your attention and once again, happy St. Louis' Day.

Title: Speech at the opening of the Session "Engaging the Haitian Diaspora as a priority for Haitian Development" of the Sixth Annual Conference of the National Alliance for the Advancement of Haitian Professionals (NAAHP) New York, 4 November 2017
text: Speech by the Governor of the Bank of the Republic of Haiti (BRH) at the opening of the Session "Engaging the Haitian Diaspora as a priority for Haitian Development" of the Sixth Annual Conference of the National Alliance for the Advancement of Haitian Professionals (NAAHP) New York, 4 November 2017 Speech by the Governor of the Bank of the Republic of Haiti (BRH) at the opening of the Session "Engaging the Haitian Diaspora as a priority for Haitian Development" of the Sixth Annual Conference of the National Alliance for the Advancement of Haitian Professionals (NAAHP) New York, 4 November 2017 Distinguished guests, colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, I would like to begin by thanking the NAAHP leaders for inviting the Bank of the Republic of Haiti to its 6th Annual Conference. The participation of the BRH in the programme is of double importance to us. First, it allows the Central Bank of Haiti to continue the dialogue it has begun with other entities of the Haitian Diaspora. It is a fruitful, vital exchange that considers, on the one hand, how to intensify the already crucial role that Haitians living abroad play in Haiti's economy. On the other hand, this dialogue offers an opportunity to suggest to these compatriots concrete ways conducive to such an intensification of their participation in production in Haiti. By exploiting the country's many potentials, we want them to benefit from existing investment opportunities in the promising and competitive sectors of the economy. Hence the second important element explaining the participation of the BRH in the meetings that bring us together today. We are pleased to have been invited to interact directly with the vibrant Haitian communities in and around major urban centers in and around the vast New York metropolitan area. It is therefore a great joy for me to greet Haitians and Haitian friends and partners living in New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, Pennsylvania, and even in Boston and New England, and beyond. A special greeting to the young professionals of the 2nd generation, so numerous in the ranks of NAAHP, and who constitute for our country of Haiti an invaluable reserve, and highly desired! I am so happy with you today! Dear friends, The theme underlying my intervention this afternoon is in line with the overall subject of the conference, namely: Diaspora and Economic Growth in Haiti: What Paths to Engagement? The development of our country requires Haiti's economy to achieve strong growth and to maintain it for years, without relenting. Without going into too much detail, it should be noted that public policies to promote this vigorous and sustained growth are broadly divided into two categories, each of which has fundamental responsibilities for any nation. These are fiscal policy and monetary policy. Tax policy is the responsibility of the Government and Parliament. Monetary policy is the responsibility of the Central Bank, which is also responsible for ensuring the stability of the national financial system and acting as the state's banker. Such a burden explains why the BRH continues to make efforts to make greater use of the significant resources at its disposal to fulfil its mission. We strive to play our part in creating this climate conducive to sustained and sustainable economic growth by stimulating private investment, including that of the Diaspora. For more than twelve years, the BRH has contributed to maintaining a relatively stable macroeconomic framework. However, high rates of economic growth, capable of lifting most of our sisters and brothers out of poverty, have not been forthcoming. BRH's acceptance of the NAAHP's invitation is part of precisely these efforts. The Central Bank conducts its mission in coordination with the economic policy framework set up by the government authorities. Another source of collaboration that we take very seriously is found in the private sector, certainly within the country, but also in our Diaspora, always faithfully present, in solidarity with the motherland. We believe that in addition to this solidarity, through your transfers, your contributions of capital and know-how, you can and must make profits in Haiti and, at the same time, promote the sustainable development of your country. That is why we are so pleased to be here with you today. The Central Bank intends to take advantage of the opportunity offered by the NAAHP conference to share with participants useful information that can help us to match the general evolution of the Haitian economic reality. Such information will help shed light on Haiti's macroeconomic framework in order to highlight the conditions conducive to maximizing viable business opportunities in promising economic sectors. But it will not be enough to share information, however useful it may be. A conference such as this provides opportunities to discover, at various levels, multiple affinities and modalities of collaboration. Based on the information provided and the experiences already acquired on the ground in Haiti, these opportunities should allow our sisters and brothers in the Diaspora, and especially our talented professionals of the 2nd generation, to be much more interested in Haiti's latent capacities. Such a development is all the more desirable as these capacities are just waiting to be fruitful in order to feed the potential of capacity building. From this point of view, it is to be hoped that the milestones laid during this conference will be seeds that, if sown wisely, will generate projects that will maximize the investment windfalls that abound in our country. The latter have also been clearly identified by both national and international expertise. Distinguished guests, My goal today is to share with you key data about the current state of the Haitian economy. This information sharing serves a dual purpose. Above all, I hope that it will lead you to appreciate the viable business opportunities offered by promising economic sectors in our country. Secondly, I also hope that the details I am going to provide will convince you to take advantage of these opportunities. My intervention will therefore have three parts: 1. First, an overview of the macroeconomic framework of our country over the last thirty-five (35) years. It will be a question of shedding a constructive light on the challenges facing us all, in order to be well imbued with the efforts that lie ahead. 2. Then, the reminder of the investment potential existing within the Haitian economy, a potential that abounds in business opportunities for a Diaspora whose unparalleled level of private transfers, and also other contributions, already make it the pillar of the Haitian economy, an invaluable reservoir of investments capable of stimulating capacity building. 3. Finally, I will analyze some examples of successful investment projects in Haiti, then I will present incentive mechanisms put in place by the Central Bank to support sectors with high productive capacity. With regard to the first part, which concerns an overview of Haiti's macroeconomic framework, I invite you to consider two sets of observations. The first is that from 1981 to 2016, the country's economy grew at an average rate of about 0.5% per year, and episodes of inflation of varying degrees of high inflation, especially during the periods 1992-1994 and 2003-2004. The economy has also suffered the stubborn effects of certain imbalances, including that of the external account, maintained by the shortcomings of exports compared to imports; and public finance imbalances, fuelled by insufficient tax revenues and volatile external aid flows. To this must be added the vagaries such as changes in the socio-political situation, the damage caused by natural disasters and the impact of external shocks such as the embargo of 1992-1994, and also external price shocks, such as those of oil and cereals. It should be noted that many of these shocks were absorbed by the Treasury deficit, resulting in significant macroeconomic imbalances. Finally, the fixed exchange rate parity, established by convention since 1919 at 5 gourdes to 1 US dollar, was abandoned in the early 90s. Thirty years later, towards the end of March 2017, the exchange rate touched the threshold of 70 gourdes to 1 dollar mainly due to these imbalances. The second set of observations is that the stabilization programmes put in place periodically by the Haitian authorities have made it possible to limit the deleterious impact of these imbalances and uncertainties. And the efforts made in recent years have led to a relative improvement in macroeconomic performance. But the great challenge for all of us remains the need to do everything possible, and on all fronts, to accelerate the pace of growth by maximizing the potential of your investments in promising sectors. This should result in a substantial improvement in the purchasing power and living conditions of the population in the long term. Dear compatriots of the Diaspora, Haiti's economic challenge is daunting, but the problems are not insurmountable. We must not give up. For its part, if the BRH is clearly aware of the challenges facing our country, it is to signal the urgency of getting to work without delay and redoubling its efforts to meet these challenges, once and for all. In this perspective, the Central Bank of Haiti is simply an institution at the service of the progress of our country, with a view to an inclusive Haiti. It sees itself as a link in a large national chain, a partner among many, ready to bring a frank collaboration to any development effort in accordance with its statutory attributions. And this idea gives me the opportunity to move on to the second part of this presentation, to recall both the good prospects of the Haitian economy, and the place that must play this indispensable partner that is the Diaspora. In terms of good prospects, consider the following four (4) performance indicators: 1. The average annual growth rate of the economy has hovered around 2% over the past 5 years, and a more robust result is expected for the 2017-2018 fiscal year. 2. In the fiscal year just ended (2016-2017), net foreign exchange reserves increased to over the billion-dollar threshold. 3. The exchange rate deviated from the 70 gourdes to the dollar mark it had almost touched at the end of March 2017, to gradually decline and reach 62.47 gourdes to the dollar at the end of July, a level at which it has relatively stabilized. Year-on-year month-end inflation, while still relatively high compared to 2010-2014 levels (around 5%), returned from the upward slope followed by February 2017 (13.9%) to June (15.8%), stabilizing at 15.6% in July and 15.4% in September. It should be noted that this inflation rate is mainly attributable to the residual effects of the impact of Hurricane Matthew on agricultural supply and to the adjustment of pump prices for petroleum products made during the 3rd quarter of the past fiscal year. 4. Monetary financing of the budget deficit was more than halved in the period from the end of FY2015 to the end of FY2016. It rose from 9.9 billion gourdes on September 30, 2015, to 4.5 billion gourdes on September 30, 2016. The improvement in the public finance situation should continue, on the one hand, with the maintenance of the cash management agreement established between the Ministry of Economy and Finance and the BRH and, on the other hand, with the gradual decrease in the significant subsidies granted by the Haitian State on the purchase of petroleum products. It should be noted that the strategy of cash management is to pursue effective management, i.e. without waste or excess, of the government's cash flows and short-term cash balances. The interventions planned by the Central Bank on the foreign exchange market should, in conjunction with other measures by both the BRH and the state authorities, help contain inflationary pressures. More generally, the current measures are more likely to succeed in the long term with the implementation of an economic recovery strategy based on the gradual orientation of these measures towards the consumption of locally produced goods and services, rather than the consumption of imported products. Such a strategy is based on a combination of three (3) factors, namely strengthening our institutions, reducing market imperfections and minimizing the major structural constraints to which our economy is subject. Reinforcing the good prospects, there are also comparative advantages that our country can claim within the Caribbean area. These benefits include: 1. The proximity of important markets, to which the country enjoys advantaged access. 2. A historical and cultural capital of an imposing richness. 3. A striking relief, composed by a geography that alternates mountains and majestic plains set with magnificent beaches, creating a framework for sustainable development, tourism in particular, including ecological and cultural. 4. A young population whose dynamism ensures the daily miracle of survival from very little, and who seeks only a minimum of possibilities and supervision to accomplish on native soil the successes achieved by his compatriots living abroad. 5. A reliable and loyal diaspora, the country's main provider of hard currency and a potential breeding ground for investors and, above all, human resources in virtually all areas. And here, we can never overemphasize the potential role of the 2nd generation, these young Haitians very attached to the land of their ancestors despite being born in the United States and elsewhere. 6. The resilience of the population, linked to ancestral values, transmitted from generation to generation, which makes Haiti, despite the negative image that persists in attributing to it, one of the safest countries on the continent, with a murder rate per 100,000 inhabitants among the lowest. Other nations in the region pride themselves on their performance in terms of foreign direct investment and tourism with much higher crime rates. But, speaking of Diaspora, what could be its contribution in the implementation of good prospects and the exploitation of comparative advantages? Let us first consider the question of the role of the Diaspora from a historical perspective. The financial contribution of the Diaspora is among the largest capital flows to Haiti, with an upward trend since the mid-1990s and a clear acceleration from 2010. Haiti is the third largest recipient of remittances in the Caribbean. Remittances from our Diaspora increased on average from 5% of gross domestic product (GDP) during the period 1992-1996, to nearly 23% of GDP over the period 2011-2016. Meanwhile, the contribution of transfers to financing Haiti's trade deficit increased on average from 27% to 70%. In 2015, transfers exceeded the flow of foreign direct investment by a multiple of 20. Since the early 2000s, remittances from Haitians living abroad have become the main component of Haiti's foreign exchange supply. Beyond this very important financial contribution, the Diaspora provides Haiti with considerable potential in terms of increased productivity, human capital formation and the development of the housing sector. Indeed, according to a study published by the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB), education represents, after food, the second largest item in the expenditure of transfer recipients. The survey highlights that the contribution of the Diaspora is equally significant in the housing sector. The evidence is clear: the uniqueness of the weight that the Diaspora has come to give itself in the economic reality of our country is indisputable. The question now is how to ensure an even deeper anchoring of the Diaspora in its homeland, particularly in terms of participation in the agenda of strong and sustained growth discussed earlier. This brings us to the 3rd and final part of my speech, which will reveal some examples of successful investment projects in Haiti. The idea is to show that, in our country, there is no shortage of business opportunities for investors, especially from the Diaspora. Next, I will describe measures developed by the BRH as an incentive to the productive sector and exports. In the case of local investments, quality financial packages have made it possible to integrate the contribution of Diaspora partners into the capital of local companies. These arrangements were carried out in three key sectors of the economy: the food industry, hotels and energy production. In addition, foreign direct investment, or FDI, has been made, with the aim of integrating local production into value chains, as in the case of the Brasserie Nationale, or Brana, and that of small millet. Other success stories were carried out with companies operating in the mobile sector and hotel establishments linked to international franchises. We cannot urge enough the deployment of foreign direct investment in Haiti. Unlike portfolio investment, FDI is not very volatile. Their impact on employment, the tax base and economic growth is more stable. In addition, FDI often generates new know-how, new technologies, new production and management techniques. They therefore contribute to enriching their sectors of activity by making them more productive and competitive, and by facilitating their access to international markets, often through their business networks. As an illustration, let's take the hotel business, which nowadays is governed by networks made up of travel agencies (real or virtual), cruise agencies, airlines, insurance services, etc. The Diaspora has every interest in seeking mechanisms that can generate projects in Haiti fueled by foreign direct investment, and also by cross-border bank loans. Such an initiative, carried out systematically under all skies where potential investors from the Diaspora meet, would help to set up the virtuous circle that will lead to the emergence of other success stories through the development of a framework where public investment will fully play its role as a catalyst for private investment, including, of course, that of the Diaspora. This is all the more urgent given that private domestic savings in Haiti are very small compared to the enormous financing needs implied by sustainable development, while the Haitian financial system has only about 1.4 billion in resources that could, when circumstances permit, be directed towards viable promising projects with a reasonable level of risk. As for the call for external savings, which combines official grants, public loans and private loans, it remains conditional on the requirements of multilateral financing agencies and the availability made possible by the economic performance of bilateral donors. It is therefore necessary to minimize certain structural and institutional constraints in order to provide direct access to private savings and, hence, to work towards the deepening of the financial market. For example, access to international capital could be promoted through the pooling of local and Diaspora resources and through the development of international guarantee instruments and other risk mitigation mechanisms. This set of constraints can be turned into opportunities for you, brothers and sisters in the Diaspora. Allow me to communicate to you, as a "policy maker" and actor evolving on the ground, the following tracks: The There is a need to improve your associative capacity around large-scale projects. The small, low-capital sole proprietorship is highly vulnerable to shocks and is subject to high operating expenses; The there are opportunities in areas with high potential for demand within the Diaspora itself, such as gated residential communities, aimed at retirees or other interested buyers. The diaspora can invest and participate in governance, by providing long-term capital or by acquiring shares in investment products such as: some growing companies, especially startups, whose evolution is limited by capital needs; some companies whose high potential is affected by all kinds of difficulties, especially capital supply; some businesses for sale or transfer of ownership; some public-private partnerships; The major multilateral financial organizations (IIC, IFC) and some bilateral donors have envelopes for promising private projects, including foreign direct investment, from which you could benefit. It is with a view to finding new solutions to stimulate investment in Haiti that BRH has implemented specific programs to promote certain productive sectors with high added value, likely to have a direct impact on employment and economic growth. These programmes to encourage the productive sector are as follows: The KAY PAM programme, set up after the earthquake of 12 January 2010 to stimulate housing credit for the middle class. It has the following characteristics: the interest rate is between 8% and 10%, and it is fixed over 10 years; The financing is denominated in gourdes, and it covers the construction, renovation and acquisition of houses. The Free Zone Development Program, established in December 2015, which focuses on increasing the country's capacity to benefit from the HOPE II and HELP Acts, which were renewed by the U.S. Senate in August 2015 for 10 years. Created in partnership with commercial banks, this program not only increases exports and the number of jobs in the textile sector, but also allows free zone promoters to obtain financing from banks on favorable terms including a maximum interest rate of 7%. The Export financing program established following memoranda of understanding signed in October 2016 by BRH with two development finance companies, the Industrial Development Fund (FDI) and the Haitian Industrial Financial Corporation for Economic and Social Development (SOFHIDES). This program promotes access to credit for enterprises producing goods and services for export. It includes a window for refinancing accounts receivable from exporters, and a credit facility to strengthen the productive capacities of targeted enterprises. This should lead in the medium to long term to the reduction of the balance of payments deficit. The A tourism and hotel incentive scheme, whereby banks are exempted from the requirement to set up minimum reserves on the resources they use to finance projects in the tourism and hospitality sectors. These sectors can thus obtain credit at more favourable interest rates. Other projects are under consideration as part of incentives for productive sectors. These include the promotion of real estate development projects, the promotion of condominiums and agricultural free zones, and the establishment of partial credit guarantees and insurance programmes for the agricultural sector. Finally, the BRH has recently embarked on a series of activities to facilitate dialogue and reflection between key players in different sectors of activity with high added value. This exercise aims to strengthen policies and financing mechanisms capable of influencing the country's economic development in a sustainable manner. Dear friends, In view of the business opportunities and support efforts of the State that I have just mentioned, I invite the Diaspora to follow the example of the predecessors who, having chosen to invest in Haiti, have for the most part already taken their place among the largest taxpayers in the country. The Diaspora has every interest in taking advantage of formulas that have proven their effectiveness. Its contribution to the development of its homeland would rise to an otherwise important level if it complemented its traditional transfers with investment-oriented initiatives in Haiti. Regional and local associations of the Diaspora could join forces with the Haitian authorities, particularly municipalities, in a logic of public/private partnership intended to finance regional development projects. Investment needs and opportunities are immense in basic socio-economic infrastructure such as education, health, drinking water distribution and renewable energy. The Diaspora could also invest directly in companies that agree to open their capital. The aim would be to promote the expansion or creation of semi-public enterprises within the framework of joint operations with institutions already involved in this type of activity, such as the Industrial Development Fund (IDF) and the International Finance Corporation (IFC). Finally, in addition to the creation of regional chambers of commerce and the establishment of business networks, the contribution of the Diaspora can also extend to trade exchanges and the transfer of skills and technology. This last aspect is particularly aimed at young professionals of the 2nd generation, whose prowess in the North American job market we have heard, and even in the boardrooms of large companies, and even in the White House of former President Barack Obama. In short, these young Haitians born outside Haiti, and whose successes on foreign lands make us all proud. Ladies and gentlemen, these are some initiatives that could gradually allow the Diaspora to maximize investment opportunities in Haiti. The Bank of the Republic of Haiti is playing its part through pro-growth measures designed to promote the productive and export sector, and to help transform the vicious circle in which we find ourselves into a virtuous cycle of strong and sustained growth, drastic reduction of poverty and continuous substantial improvement in the standard of living of the population. Thank you for your attention. Jean Baden Dubois Governor of the Bank of the Republic of Haiti

Title: Speech of the Governor of the Bank of the Republic of Haiti at the Accounting Summit  OCPAH / IFAC December 5, 2017
text: Speech of the Governor of the Bank of the Republic of Haiti at the Accounting Summit  OCPAH / IFAC December 5, 2017 Mr. Minister of Economy and Finance (Madam), Members of the IFAC delegation Ladies and gentlemen members of the Board of Directors of OCPAH (Ladies and gentlemen), Representatives of the Professional Association of Banks, (Ladies and gentlemen, Representatives of other sectors of finance, (Ladies and gentlemen representatives of the Economic Forum, Ladies and gentlemen, Dear guests, It is a great pleasure to participate in this conference. I thank the distinguished members of the Board of Directors of OCPAH for their invitation, with all the more interest and enthusiasm that accounting standards are of paramount importance in the orderly and methodical expansion of financial intermediation in Haiti, for the benefit of inclusive and stable economic growth. To the thanks I would like to add congratulations for this initiative, which is also very timely because this summit on accounting coincides with the adoption by the Bank of the Republic of Haiti and its partners of a set of measures aimed at modernizing accounting and auditing practice in Haiti. The purpose of financial statements, according to the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB), "is to provide information about the financial condition, performance and changes in the financial position of an entity that is useful to a wide range of users in making economic decisions." Indeed, accounting standards are authoritative rules for financial reporting. They specify how transactions and other events are to be recognized, measured, reported and reported in the financial statements. They are intended to provide investors, lenders, creditors and others with financial information that is useful in assessing the company's ability to generate value. Accounting standardization therefore makes it possible to enact common methods, conventions, rules and principles that are supposed to be binding on all economic entities. It offers a certain rationality that guarantees seriousness and rigour in evaluations, but it provides the basis on which users can base their judgment on the quality of accounting information. In other words, standardization is the pillar of any accounting system, in the sense that it codifies the accounting production process, control and verification mechanisms. The International Financial Reporting Standards  or IFRS for short  promote, or at least support, a financialized economy without borders. Particularly oriented towards the information needs of shareholders and stock market investors, this financial reporting is an instrument for monitoring and evaluating the decisions of managers. Ladies and Gentlemen The importance of accounting has been repeatedly illustrated in recent years, often by high-profile scandals such as Enron, WorldCom, AIG or Parmalat. It is in this context that Mr. Hank Paulson, former Secretary of the Treasury (between July 2006 and January 2009), described accounting as "the lifeblood of financial markets". In a world where the complexity of financial transactions is becoming increasingly impressive, accounting provides the foundation for the trust on which capital markets are based. When financial data can no longer be trusted, the entire market edifice is threatened. The development of accounting standards is therefore a form of economic policy because as the economy becomes more complex, the choice of what is measured becomes increasingly difficult and decisive. Accounting, once seen as a mere means of proof, has become an indispensable tool in the service of information whose ultimate objective is to assist and facilitate decision-making. The quality of financial information is in first place among the factors of choice for investors. This information is largely accounting at the origin and it is quite natural that we seek to develop international standards that will allow in addition to obtaining information but also objects of transactions. In this sense, international accounting standards are of paramount importance for the financial sector, going beyond the purely accounting framework to address corporate governance requirements and, in particular, the need to report on actions taken, decisions taken and their impact on the creation of economic value. Ladies and Gentlemen, Modernizing and stabilizing the national economy and in particular the financial sector are primary objectives for the Bank of the Republic of Haiti. A number of measures taken to date allow the BRH to ensure that the regulations in force in the banking sector are in line with certain international good accounting practices. However, the accounting practice in Haiti requires significant strengthening in order to promote a business climate favourable to private investment and access for companies to credit and long-term financing. BRH's action is therefore part of this desire to facilitate greater transparency of financial information, which inevitably involves the adoption and application of accounting standards that correspond a little more to current economic realities. Given globalization, the adoption of internationally recognized accounting standards will promote Haitian companies' access to global capital markets, without the significant out-of-pocket costs of restating their financial statements. Over the past two decades, the globalization of trade and financial markets has changed the way financial assets are managed, eliminated barriers between markets and increased investor choice. Our companies have an opportunity to grow with capital from a wider range of investors, with positive effects on the country's economic development. Companies, particularly financial firms, wishing to attract capital should present and disclose their financial information in a repository that is easy to read and interpret. Ultimately, financial sector companies seeking access to the global fund market for growth and expansion should implement international standards as soon as possible. Financial globalization is pushing us to change the paradigm and today we want to announce a change of course in terms of adopting international accounting standards or adapting them to our economic reality, because all the actors concerned must combine their efforts to provide the country with an appropriate accounting framework close to IFRS or to adopt them altogether. We know, in fact, that the adoption of IFRS standards at the national level, particularly at the level of the banking system, is part of a vast project that must naturally be carried out in stages and follow a sequence of appropriate actions including priority actions and medium- and long-term objectives. Nevertheless, on the basis of diagnoses already established and the recommendations made, we believe that it is necessary to carry out a rapid inventory in order to identify the priority actions to be undertaken in the short, medium and long term. It is in this perspective that the Central Bank, together with the entities concerned (the MEF and the OCPAH), will work on the establishment of a national action plan that will set the main objectives to be achieved in order to provide the country with an accounting framework that can contribute to improving the financial transparency of companies. BRH is already working on a strategy to improve accounting and auditing practices in Haiti. The main objectives pursued are the strengthening of OCPAH's organizational capacities and the opening of the audit market (financial and technological). The aim here is to have a quality service offer in this sector that will help stabilize the financial system and facilitate access to credit for small and medium-sized enterprises. In short, ladies and gentlemen, in its desire to develop, modernize and strengthen the national financial market, the BRH is already beginning to lay the groundwork for the creation of a capital market in Haiti. Like the adoption of an accounting framework, there are structural and institutional constraints that will have to be removed to promote access to international capital for Haitian companies. It is therefore essential that commercial, financial or other enterprises wishing to call on national and/or international private savings provide investors and other stakeholders with quantitative information, as objective as possible, enabling them to assess the quantity and quality of value created. In this context, international accounting standards are of paramount importance to the financial sector as they can facilitate the mobilization of capital for companies and contribute to the creation of economic value. As a result, there is a need for diligent action to improve accounting practice in the country. As I mentioned above, we must agree that the work is great but thanks to a combination of the forces and means of all the actors concerned, we will be able to initiate all the changes likely to lead us towards convergence with international standards. The Bank of the Republic of Haiti is already doing and will do everything in its power to strengthen the accounting profession in Haiti and improve the overall investment climate. It will continue to support the financial sector by creating a framework conducive to the development of companies in this sector. I remain convinced that the positions expressed at this summit will be worthwhile and that the results of the work that will follow will be palpable in a short time. Thank you. Jean Baden Dubois Governor of the Bank of the Republic of Haiti

Title: Speech at the opening ceremony of the 2nd Conference on Decentralized Franco-Haitian Cooperation Tuesday 5 and Wednesday 6 December 2017
text: Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois at the opening ceremony of the 2nd Conference on Franco-Haitian Decentralized Cooperation Tuesday 5 and Wednesday 6 December 2017 Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois at the opening ceremony of the 2nd Conference on Decentralized Franco-Haitian Cooperation Tuesday 5 and Wednesday 6 December 2017 Members of the Three Powers; The Mayor of Port-au-Prince; Dear Colleagues of the BRH Board of Directors; Mr. President of the National Federation of Mayors of Haiti; Ambassador of France to Haiti; Mr. President of the Haiti Country Group; Distinguished Representatives of partner institutions and organizations; Ladies and gentlemen, representatives of the press; Distinguished participants; Honourable guests; Ladies and gentlemen It gives me great pleasure to welcome you to this opening ceremony of the 2nd Conference on Decentralized Franco-Haitian Cooperation. And it is with great enthusiasm that the Bank of the Republic of Haiti (BRH) joins this initiative as a partner and host of this event, which benefits from the support of the President of the Republic who wanted to enhance his presence at this morning's conference. We welcome with equal warmth the eminent foreign personalities who, once again, have shown us their friendship by coming to participate in these exchanges, here at the BRH Convention Centre. I would particularly like to thank Ambassador de France, Elisabeth Beton Delegue, for having kindly assisted the interest that our local elected representatives attach to the cooperation agreements to which this conference will give rise. I join in the same testimony of thanks the Federation of Mayors of Haiti (FENAMH), the Ministry of the Interior and Territorial Communities (MICT) as well as the Haitian executives who will lend themselves to this exercise of exchange of expertise and knowledge during the thematic sessions and workshops planned. Honourable guests; Ladies and gentlemen; The organization of this conference in this chamber is a source of pride for us insofar as the earthquake had left a field of ruins in the city center. Not far from the headquarters of the PAP City Council, this building and its architectural particularity have become today the sign of a firm commitment to the revitalization of the commercial and administrative center of the capital and in the entire process of reconstruction of the country in which all municipalities have their role to play. The holding of this work is, of course, a privileged moment of benevolent cordiality and unprecedented meetings, but it is also, in my view, a reaffirmation of the will of our communities to strengthen the network of mutual aid on issues of major interest to our two countries and to the environment. These are issues that touch on the essentials, the future of our planet, and that are at the forefront of the concerns of any responsible government, whether local or national: climate change and the prevention of natural risks, spatial planning, tourism and cultural heritage, education and vocational training, the pooling of means and resources, water and sanitation management, civil society and democracy, waste management, agriculture, agro-ecology and rural development, local taxation and territorial autonomy, cross-border cooperation, the challenges and specificity of Caribbean regional cooperation. All these themes are important. However, I would like to make a few comments on a point that does not seem to be on the menu of this conference and that deserves to be debated. This is internal migration, i.e. population movements within the country. It seems to me that the mayors of large cities should consider that the large share they hold in the national budget is an additional attraction towards large agglomerations with all the risks that this represents. I therefore encourage the central government and FENAMH to help the less well-endowed (adjoining) cities to equip themselves with adequate resources within the framework of fair and equitable equalization. Development must be primarily rural if we want to avoid concentrations of increasingly vulnerable populations in urban areas. Two of the themes mentioned above are at the heart of the Haitian problem: the prevention of natural risks, education and vocational training. On the first subject, the BRH's room for manoeuvre is limited, from a legal point of view, with regard to its statutory missions. Nevertheless, support for the private sector through, among other things, the access of Haitian youth to education and vocational and academic training of quality and high level is one of the privileged areas of intervention of the Board of Directors that I have the honor to chair. In this regard, the BRH is pleased to have welcomed on August 24, 2017 to the Convention Center a delegation of students selected as part of the BRH Scholarships program for France-Haiti friendship, initiated by the Haitian Parliament and supported by BRH and France. On this occasion, I reiterated BRH's commitment to continue investing in human capital in order to provide the country with more qualified executives, for the benefit of better competitiveness and sustained growth. Our institution is one of those who believe that Haiti needs to see the emergence of young leaders capable of carrying out innovative projects and leading the way to economic prosperity and sustainable development. In other words, if it develops and expands, decentralized Franco-Haitian cooperation can become an important lever for BRH's action in terms of capacity building and human capital development in its pro-growth monetary policy approach. Honourable guests; Ladies and gentlemen; This meeting is therefore another opportunity for our institution to take stock of its contribution to improving human capital in a context where many Haitian families make immense sacrifices to finance the studies and installation costs of their children abroad. Indeed, Haiti transferred during the 2016-2017 fiscal year more than 250 million US dollars to the rest of the world. These transfers include, to a large extent, the financing of higher and technical studies. This amount may seem insignificant for a country like France, but it represents 12.5% of the national budget and more than 8 times the investment made for the establishment of the University of Lemonade in the North. In other words, if we could add 3 points more to the current tax burden to bring it to 15% of GDP estimated at 8 billion dollars, it would be possible to have at least one large university center in the district capital of each department of the country. Given the positive externalities associated with education, this would allow us to produce a critical mass of lawyers, doctors, engineers, agronomists, economists and financiers that FENAMH so badly needs for its local development projects. This fiscal effort is particularly necessary for local authorities given the low collection rate observed in the country's 146 municipalities. Indeed, the tax administration is not very efficient, and in some municipalities there have been significant variations in revenue with the arrival of new local leaders. This means that it is absolutely important to redress the situation of local finances to allow mayors to invest in profitable economic activities that will in turn contribute to the broadening of the local tax base. Similarly, as indicated above, an equalization effort is essential to take into account the differences between the fiscal potential of rich and poor municipalities in order to promote an overall dynamic in the preparation and implementation of development projects and thus create conditions for the financial inclusion of vulnerable segments of the population. In other words, fiscal recovery and tax fairness are public goods and represent the only possible solutions to protect populations and avoid cases elsewhere, where the state has experienced bankruptcies following the accumulation of budget deficits in local governments on top of the central government deficit. It also gives us an idea of the efforts we need to make to fund knowledge through smart, results-oriented cooperation. I have no doubt that we can achieve this, because as Leopold Sedar Senghor said so well: "in the appointment of giving and receiving, we will not come empty-handed". In view of these considerations, it is quite possible to envisage decentralized cooperation as a powerful development tool integrating not only grants and loans in support of the budget, but also coherent budgetary choices, public-private partnerships and the raising of investment funds through municipal vouchers for large-scale projects. This gives me the opportunity to look back at BRH's pro-growth programs that offer new opportunities for mayors capable of improving governance in their region. Because, in terms of funding, potential partners are looking for "success stories" that technology can relay through social media and conferences such as those that bring us together in this building this morning and all the others that will take place after. You therefore have, ladies and gentlemen mayors of Haiti, evidence of the roadmap that should allow you, at the end of this conference, to ensure in the best possible conditions, the follow-up and implementation of the resolutions that have been taken. It is with these words of commitment that I conclude my remarks by wishing you two good and fruitful days of work. Jean Baden Dubois Governor of the Bank of the Republic of Haiti

Title: Speech at the closing ceremony of the "Economy for Journalists" programme Thursday, December 7, 2017
text: Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois at the closing ceremony of the "Economy for Journalists" programme Thursday, December 7, 2017 Dear Members of the Board of Directors, Mr. Director General of the Ministry of Economy and Finance, Mrs. Resident Representative of the World Bank, Mr. CEO of the Growth Group, Ladies and Gentlemen Media Directors, Ladies and Gentlemen Directors and Executives of the Bank of the Republic of Haiti, Ladies and Gentlemen Trainers and Speakers, Ladies and gentlemen, journalists/participants of the training program, Dear guests Ladies / Gentlemen I take great pleasure in closing today the series of interventions, sometimes masterful and sometimes more participatory, which marked the training provided as part of our "Economy for Journalists" program. It is a training that can validly be described as a long cycle since, spread over a period of nine months and supplemented by a didactic approach that responds both to academic concerns, as regards theoretical baggage, and to practical concerns, as to the subtleties involved in the implementation of economic programmes and the implementation of policies defined in particular within the framework of external cooperation. I deliberately place today's ceremony in the broader perspective of the interventions that marked these nine months of training to emphasize the established fact that, for the practitioner as for the academic, the satisfactory understanding of socio-economic phenomena results from a continuous learning that finds anchoring in the mastery and renewal of knowledge on a reality itself in constant change. It could not be otherwise for the journalist who acts as a bridge between the public policy maker who is the practitioner, and the beneficiary of public policies, who is the public, the community. The columnist, the communicator, the columnist, the analyst or in general the opinion director that you are, is an essential figure in this noble body of profession that gives substance to what has rightly been called the field of public policy. So you understand my insistence on spreading the idea that this ceremony dedicates an open door to a continuous learning process at a time when the speed, complexity, density and virtually infinite horizon of available information force innovative reflection and action more today than yesterday and even more when it comes to putting into perspective what we all want from our society tomorrow. Ladies and gentlemen, Welcome to the closing ceremony of the first edition of our "Economy for Journalists" programme. I beg your indulgence to address my customary greetings to you only at this rather late stage of my speech, you would rightly say. I wanted my introductory remarks to be sufficiently introductory to challenge everyone in a singular way  if you will pardon the redundancy  to challenge everyone on the need to significantly improve the dissemination, understanding and effectiveness of our public policies. Allow me to thank emphatically the senior state clerks and media managers who responded to our invitation. They represent the first level of leadership in the chain of transmission of public policy signals and reponsives. Secondly, I hasten to greet the executives of the administrations and the journalists of the various media. They are the linchpin of this transmission. On behalf of the Board of Directors, I congratulate the trainers of this program for having lived up to expectations and the journalists recipients whose interest and incisive spirit have made it possible to raise the quality of exchanges and the level of training. We have entered an era of cooperation that goes beyond the strict scope of the orthodox activities of a Central Bank in the management of the city. Quoted obviously taken in its etymological sense. "Economy for Journalists" is a first. I am proud to have the chance to be an actor in this initiative that paves the way for this field of cooperation and I would like this pride to be contagious. Ladies and Gentlemen, Today's ceremony would lose its purpose if it does not emphasize the expectations of the monetary authority of this open field of cooperation with the media. This is a major obligation because, as promised in my opening remarks, I want to place today's ceremony in the broader perspective of the interventions that have marked these nine months of fruitful training sessions. Therefore, allow me to explain the objectives pursued by the Bank of the Republic of Haiti through this initiative. 1. First, the level of dialogue between all decision-makers in the financial system and the public must be raised by establishing a viable space for intermediation in the (dissemination) transmission of economic and financial information. In the coming days ladies and gentlemen and throughout the year 2018, the BRH will rise to raise the level of dialogue in the general public through a very mediatic program of Financial Education, which is an integral part of our National Strategy of Financial Inclusion. Today, the culmination of nine months of training under the "Economy for Journalists" programme raises the bar to a higher level. It reveals the establishment of a new and important part of the activities of the Central Bank in its renewed quest for the effectiveness of monetary policy and the development of the financial system. We recognize the fundamental role that well-processed and digested information is called upon to play in amplifying well-thought-out public policy measures. It helps to shorten reaction times and to condition reflexes in the expected direction of these reactions. It also helps to balance these reactions according to the degree of the issues at stake, in particular, by reducing the often unjustified runaways of the market to more reasonable proportions. A disciplined, educated and well-informed public is therefore a major asset for the informed and well-equipped policy-maker. The Central Bank has worked to make this approach a strategy. The creation at the beginning of this year 2017 of the Communication Department responds to this imperative. 2. Secondly, it is a question of reducing the asymmetry of information in order to promote a better formation of expectations and of creating the conditions that allow public policies to benefit fairly quickly from the fruits of a communication approach set up as a strategic function. One of the fundamental lessons of containing the first waves of the 2008 financial crisis in the United States of America was the importance of the communication function in the effectiveness of Moral Persuasion as an instrument in the field of public policy. In Haiti, the resolution of currency crises of varying magnitudes over the past twenty years confirms the importance of the communication function in the central banker's toolbox. These episodes of crisis have shown the capacity of moral suasion to contain negative expectations driven mainly by deliberate misinformation and extra-economic considerations. So many experiences that have fed this fund of analysis that has earned us today the systematization of this approach of service to the community of the Central Bank. By making this approach institutional, the Bank of the Republic intends to introduce a scale factor in the conduct of policies that meet its missions. At a time when we want monetary policy to take a more engaging stance in relation to the growth environment, the Central Bank cannot avoid a function as important as that of communication. And we strongly expect the dividends in terms of the synergy and amplification effects sought in the implementation of the measures enshrined in our vision of monetary policy. Dear recipients, you are therefore at the forefront of an approach that makes you privileged partners of a new deal in the conduct of monetary policy in Haiti. You will therefore have to sensitize economic actors objectively and without bias on the role of information in general and economic information in particular in the process that leads to decision-making. In doing so, you will carve out a place for yourself in the ongoing approach that aims to reduce the asymmetry of economic and financial information for a better formation of expectations and motivations that guide the choices of consumers and investors. If only 20% of unrequited transfers could be invested in production instead of consumption, our economic environment would be greatly improved. That would be direct investments of over 400 million each year... Far greater than all the aid received for the 2016-2017 fiscal year (387 million including budget support) Finally, in line with the FED Watchers who are working to decode the signals launched by the Federal Reserve in the United States to make them accessible to economic actors, I see with happiness, the creation, in the long term, of a group of BRH Watchers and more broadly of Public Policy Watchers called upon to inform Haitian economic actors on the ins and outs of the explicit and unspoken elements of public policy measures. Ladies and Gentlemen, It is therefore obvious that we are not going to stop there. We intend to continue our information and training activities not only in the capital, but also in the various departments of the country. We are already planning for this first class of 17 journalists sessions to recall, strengthen and renew the knowledge acquired. The prospect of a Level II course, seminars led by international experts and other projects is also envisaged. Before concluding, I would like to reiterate my thanks to all the professors and lecturers who have had to intervene in this program and especially to the IFBC who designed, planned and implemented this program with professionalism and passion. I want to thank in a special way Mr. Ronald Gabriel who was at the level of the Board of Directors the linchpin of this training and I ask you to applaud him. Once again, congratulations from the Board of Directors to the recipients and media directors who made the sacrifice of making them available for our program. Thank you!

Title: Speech at the dividend delivery ceremony by NATCOM to the Haitian State
text: Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois at the dividend ceremony by NATCOM to the Haitian State Speech by Governor Jean Baden Dubois at the dividend delivery ceremony by NATCOM to the Haitian State Honourable Members Mr Secretary of State for Finance Mr. Managing Director of Natcom Dear colleagues of the Board of Directors of BRH Mr. Director General of CONATEL Distinguished members of the Press, Today is an important step that is taken after 7 years of collaboration between Natcom and the Haitian State. Because this company, of which the State owns 40%, is making its dividend declaration to the Haitian State for the first time, through the BRH, of which I have the honor to chair the Board of Directors. Ladies and Gentlemen Allow me to pay tribute to the work done by the entire Natcom team, which has been able, with dynamism and professionalism, to make the institution what it is today in the mobile telephony market. Allow me to thank the Board of Directors of NATCOM represented by Viettel and BRH who worked to implement strategic policies to improve the quality of services offered to the population and also presented interesting plans for all budgets. Working in the common interest, providing quality service at an affordable price must be the credo of Natcom and that is why we seek the collaboration of everyone to make the Company stronger and more profitable. Natcom also belongs to Haiti! It is a national company. Every Haitian has an interest in appropriating this mixed company so that it can bring dividends to the Haitian State and contribute to the increase in tax revenues. Today, Natcom also wants to contribute to providing the country with qualified executives, so the Board of Directors has strongly supported and obtained from Viettel the granting of thirty scholarships for engineering training to young Haitians who will have the opportunity to specialize in the fields of Engineering and Technology in international Vietnamese universities. This project, the modalities of which will be defined by Viettel and the Haitian State, is very important for us at the Central Bank because these young students will have the opportunity to familiarize themselves with the entrepreneurial culture of Vietnam, a country that is experiencing increasingly sustained economic growth. The training of these students in Vietnamese universities must also promote Haitian integration on the technical level in the company. Once again, I invite you dear fellow citizens to use the services of Natcom, of which the Haitian State holds 40% of the shares through the BRH. Thank you
